text:
The Taming of the Shrew – William Shakespeare
‘Audiences enjoy the ways in which Petruchio takes charge.’
In the light of this view, discuss how Shakespeare presents Petruchio in this extract and
elsewhere in the play.
[25 marks]
PETRUCHIO
Now, Kate, I am a husband for your turn,
For by this light whereby I see thy beauty,
Thy beauty that doth make me like thee well,
Thou must be married to no man but me.
For I am he am born to tame you, Kate,
And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate
Conformable as other household Kates.
Enter Baptista, Gremio, and Tranio
Here comes your father. Never make denial;
I must and will have Katherine to my wife.
BAPTISTA
Now, Signor Petruchio, how speed you with my daughter?
PETRUCHIO
How but well, sir? How but well?
It were impossible I should speed amiss.
BAPTISTA
Why, how now, daughter Katherine? In your dumps?
KATHERINA
Call you me daughter? Now I promise you
You have showed a tender fatherly regard
To wish me wed to one half lunatic,
A madcap ruffian and a swearing Jack,
That thinks with oaths to face the matter out.
PETRUCHIO
Father, ’tis thus — yourself and all the world
That talked of her have talked amiss of her.
If she be curst, it is for policy,
For she’s not froward, but modest as the dove.
She is not hot, but temperate as the morn.
For patience she will prove a second Grissel,
And Roman Lucrece for her chastity.
And to conclude, we have ’greed so well together
That upon Sunday is the wedding-day.
KATHERINA
I’ll see thee hanged on Sunday first.
GREMIO
Hark, Petruchio, she says she’ll see thee hanged first.
TRANIO
Is this your speeding? Nay then, good night our part.
PETRUCHIO
Be patient, gentlemen, I choose her for myself.
If she and I be pleased, what’s that to you?
’Tis bargained ’twixt us twain, being alone,
That she shall still be curst in company.
I tell you ’tis incredible to believe
How much she loves me – O, the kindest Kate!
She hung about my neck, and kiss on kiss
She vied so fast, protesting oath on oath,
That in a twink she won me to her love.
O, you are novices! ’Tis a world to see
How tame, when men and women are alone,
A meacock wretch can make the curstest shrew.
Give me thy hand, Kate, I will unto Venice,
To buy apparel ’gainst the wedding-day.
Provide the feast, father, and bid the guests.
I will be sure my Katherine shall be fine.
BAPTISTA
I know not what to say – but give me your hands.
God send you joy! Petruchio, ’tis a match.
GREMIO and TRANIO
Amen, say we. We will be witnesses.
PETRUCHIO
Father, and wife, and gentlemen, adieu,
I will to Venice – Sunday comes apace.
We will have rings, and things, and fine array,
And kiss me, Kate, we will be married o’ Sunday.
Exeunt Petruchio and Katherina
(Act 2, Scene 1)
msText:
Question 02
The Taming of the Shrew – William Shakespeare
‘Audiences enjoy the ways in which Petruchio takes charge.’
In the light of this view, discuss how Shakespeare presents Petruchio in this extract and
elsewhere in the play.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Students might consider:
• the view that Petruchio taking charge and his ability to win over both Katherina and Baptista is part
of his charm and energy which the audience enjoys
• the ways he directs events and also the course of his relationship with Katherina
• the ways he addresses Katherina – complimenting her, directly addressing her as his confidante,
etc
• the ways in which he talks about Katherina to others – turning negatives about her as a shrew into
positive attributes as a woman, insisting that she is loving and that she seduced him in private
• that their love is their private business, etc
• the ways in which he is ‘speeding’ and eager to announce their forthcoming marriage
• the theatricality of Petruchio as ‘director’/‘stage manager’ and ‘performer’
• the apparent enthusiasm of Baptista, Gremio and Tranio by the end
• the apparent compliance of Katherina, suggested by her silence in the second half of the scene
• the alternative view that these qualities are tools of control and manipulation to ensure that he wins
the dowry and control of his wife
• the view that an audience of the time may have enjoyed his behaviour but increasingly he may be
viewed by audiences as a repellently controlling patriarch
• the alternative view that he is ‘railroading’ the situation by using lies and exaggerations
• the view that Petruchio is, in fact, the ‘madcap ruffian’ and ‘swearing Jack’ Katherina claims him to
be
• scenes elsewhere that arguably present Petruchio as a cruel abuser
• scenes elsewhere in the play that facilitate the debate about Petruchio’s possible effect on the
audience and the other characters
• the use of ‘audiences’, ‘enjoys’, ‘the ways’, ‘takes charge’ in the given view
• the comic genre
• the possible impact of particular production(s) on the interpretation of the question
• the possible impact of recent debates about the exploitation of women and the controlling nature of
men
• etc.
AO4 Explore connections across literary texts
Focus might be on (in the literature of love):
• representations of: (male) control of a love partner; a lover’s use of charm, wit and energy to get
their own way; lovers’ preparations for marriage; enthusiastic lovers, or the opposite; boastful
lovers; family scenes involving parents
• the comedic genre
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• how attitudes to the following might have changed over time: the expectations of husbands, wives
and love within a marriage; ideas about patriarchal dominance; the importance of parental approval
• the comedic context
• etc.
AO2 Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in literary texts
Focus might be on:
• the comedy genre
• possible stage effects and interpretations
• structural issues relating to this stage of the plot: the early stages of the ‘taming’ process where
Petruchio appears to believe that the force of his will and personality will ensure early success
• the ways in which the verse reflects the subject matter and attitude of the speakers, particularly:
Petruchio’s dominance of the stage and conversations; the different techniques and styles he
adopts towards Katherina, Baptista, Gremio and Tranio; Petruchio’s relentless enthusiasm,
boastfulness and idealism in the face of Katherina’s sarcasm, the joking of Gremio and Tranio, and
Baptista’s questions
• the ways in which Petruchio uses language to take charge and exercise control
• the use of enjambement and caesurae to reflect the arguments of the speakers
• the rhetorical devices used particularly by Petruchio, such as: patterns of repetition; the wordplay
around epithets for Katherina (echoed by her descriptions of him); his use of superlatives,
apostrophe, etc.
• Petruchio’s quick-fire ripostes and commands to others while he builds an idealised narrative of his
wedding to Katherina
• the various ways in which Petruchio conveys the briskness, simplicity and certainty of his plans
• the bathos created by juxtaposing Petruchio’s enthusiasm with the realism of Katherina’s
responses
• the ways in which he fluctuates between ‘Katherine’ and ‘Kate’
• the various ways in which the syntax of statements, questions, exclamations and commands, along
with various forms of repetition, are used to underline thoughts, feelings and attitudes
• the roles of Gremio and Tranio in providing a bantering chorus
• irony and dramatic irony
• etc.
AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression
• quality of argument
• organisation of ideas
• use of appropriate concepts and terminology
• technical accuracy.
Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of
authorial methods.
erText: The Taming of the Shrew Extract from Act 2, Scene 1: ‘Audiences enjoy the ways in which Petruchio takes charge.’ In the light of this view, discuss how Shakespeare presents Petruchio in this extract and elsewhere in the play. What students did well • considered Petruchio’s speech and behaviour in the context of the play as a comedy. • examined different attitudes over time to the idea of a man taking charge. • concentrated on ‘ways’ in the plural, allowing for slapstick comedy, for example, in other scenes. • explored other readings of Petruchio including that the idea that he, too, is tamed and made to appreciate love. • alluded to scenes where he is working with others, including sharing jokes with Katherina, rather than seeking to control. • kept ‘audiences’ and the dramatic context in focus. Common misunderstandings • wrote a character study of Petruchio. • described/narrated the taming process. • neglected the comedic genre to discuss Petruchio as no more than a materialistic, misogynistic abuser and Katherina as no more than a passive victim.

text:
Measure for Measure – William Shakespeare
‘In Measure for Measure, the trust between men and women is completely broken.’
In the light of this view, discuss how Shakespeare presents relationships between men
and women in this extract and elsewhere in the play.
[25 marks]
IV.4
Enter Angelo and Escalus
ESCALUS Every letter he hath writ hath disvouched other.
ANGELO In most uneven and distracted manner. His
actions show much like to madness. Pray heaven his
wisdom be not tainted. And why meet him at the gates,
and reliver our authorities there?
ESCALUS I guess not.
ANGELO And why should we proclaim it in an hour before
his entering, that if any crave redress of injustice, they
should exhibit their petitions in the street?
ESCALUS He shows his reason for that – to have a dispatch
of complaints, and to deliver us from devices hereafter,
which shall then have no power to stand against us.
ANGELO
Well, I beseech you let it be proclaimed.
Betimes i’th’morn I’ll call you at your house.
Give notice to such men of sort and suit
As are to meet him.
ESCALUS
I shall, sir. Fare you well.
ANGELO
Good night.
Exit Escalus
This deed unshapes me quite, makes me unpregnant
And dull to all proceedings. A deflowered maid,
And by an eminent body that enforced
The law against it! But that her tender shame
Will not proclaim against her maiden loss,
How might she tongue me? Yet reason dares her no,
For my authority bears so credent bulk
That no particular scandal once can touch
But it confounds the breather. He should have lived,
Save that his riotous youth with dangerous sense
Might in the times to come have ta’en revenge,
By so receiving a dishonoured life
With ransom of such shame. Would yet he had lived.
Alack, when once our grace we have forgot,
Nothing goes right. We would, and we would not.
Exit
IV.6
Enter Isabella and Mariana
ISABELLA
To speak so indirectly I am loath.
I would say the truth, but to accuse him so,
That is your part. Yet I am advised to do it,
He says, to veil full purpose.
MARIANA
Be ruled by him.
ISABELLA
Besides, he tells me that if peradventure
He speak against me on the adverse side,
I should not think it strange, for ’tis a physic
That’s bitter to sweet end.
MARIANA
I would Friar Peter –
Enter Friar Peter
ISABELLA
O, peace, the friar is come.
FRIAR PETER
Come, I have found you out a stand most fit,
Where you may have such vantage on the Duke
He shall not pass you. Twice have the trumpets
sounded.
The generous and gravest citizens
Have hent the gates, and very near upon
The Duke is entering. Therefore hence, away. Exeunt
(Act 4, Scene 4 and Scene 6)

Question 03
Measure for Measure – William Shakespeare
‘In Measure for Measure, the trust between men and women is completely broken.’
In the light of this view, discuss how Shakespeare presents relationships between men
and women in this extract and elsewhere in the play.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Students might consider:
• scenes 4 and 6 separately or conflated together as one extract; students should not be penalised
for dealing with scenes unequally
• the view that trust between men and women has been broken in different relationships – between
siblings such as Claudio and Isabella; between lovers or potential lovers such as Angelo and
Mariana; between male leaders such as the Duke and Angelo and their female subjects, Isabella
for example
• Angelo’s belief that, despite his corruption, he remains untouchable and that the Duke is seeking to
protect him
• his belief that he had to renege on the promise to save Claudio in order to protect himself
• his awareness that he may be denied grace because of his guilt as sexual predator and unlawful
killer
• the fact that Angelo continues to neglect Mariana, his betrothed
• the view that the Duke’s disguise and deception as the Friar undermines trust between men and
women even while he contrives to do good
• the view that the Duke’s return and plans do not restore trust because he merely contrives a series
of marriages at the end
• the alternative view that the Duke, as the Friar, is working to right Angelo’s wrongs and will restore
faith in authority and justice
• the Duke’s reported pledge to Isabella that she will be protected in speaking out against Angelo
• the Duke’s reported hint to Isabella that he may have to appear to support Angelo initially but that
she will be saved
• the ways in which Friar Peter is presented as a supportive figure of trust in Scene 6
• the way in which the supportive co-operation and trust between Isabella and Mariana thrives
despite Angelo’s corrupt rule
• the view that the later revelation of the bed trick, reunion and a sanctioned marriage between
Angelo and Mariana after her return mends the damage done to trust
• these two scenes as part of a coherent narrative strand at this point in the play
• other scenes where Angelo’s destructive behaviour is presented
• the use of ‘trust’ and ‘completely broken’ in the given view
• the tragicomedy/problem play genre
• the possible impact of particular production(s) on the interpretation of the question
• the possible impact of recent debates about the exploitation of women and the controlling nature of
men
• etc.
AO4 Explore connections across literary texts
Focus might be on (in the literature of love):
• representations of: characters and events that break/restore trusting relationship between men and
women, particularly lovers; unmasking the truth about infidelity/abuse
• the tragicomedy/problem play genre
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• how attitudes to the following might have changed over time: expectations about the honour and
morality of those in positions of responsibility; unmasking the truth about infidelity/abuse;

• etc.

preparations for the Duke’s arrival bringing the play to a dramatic and morally restorative

his soliloquy; the ways in which Shakespeare presents the intertwined causes of Isabella and

text:
The Winter’s Tale – William Shakespeare
‘The extent of Leontes’ grief completely restores sympathy for him.’
In the light of this view, discuss how Shakespeare presents thoughts and feelings about
Leontes’ past actions in this extract and elsewhere in the play.
[25 marks]
LEONTES
O Paulina,
We honour you with trouble. But we came
To see the statue of our queen: your gallery
Have we passed through, not without much content
In many singularities; but we saw not
That which my daughter came to look upon,
The statue of her mother.
PAULINA
As she lived peerless,
So her dead likeness I do well believe
Excels whatever yet you looked upon,
Or hand of man hath done; therefore I keep it
Lonely, apart. But here it is: prepare
To see the life as lively mocked as ever
Still sleep mocked death. Behold, and say ’tis well!
Paulina draws a curtain and reveals Hermione, stand-
ing like a statue
I like your silence: it the more shows off
Your wonder. But yet speak: first you, my liege.
Comes it not something near?
LEONTES
Her natural posture!
Chide me, dear stone, that I may say indeed
Thou art Hermione; or rather, thou art she
In thy not chiding, for she was as tender
As infancy and grace. But yet, Paulina,
Hermione was not so much wrinkled, nothing
So agèd as this seems.
POLIXENES
O, not by much!
PAULINA
So much the more our carver’s excellence,
Which lets go by some sixteen years and makes her
As she lived now.
LEONTES
As now she might have done,
So much to my good comfort as it is
Now piercing to my soul. O, thus she stood,
Even with such life of majesty – warm life,
As now it coldly stands – when first I wooed her!
I am ashamed. Does not the stone rebuke me
For being more stone than it? O royal piece!
There’s magic in thy majesty, which has
My evils conjured to remembrance, and
From thy admiring daughter took the spirits,
Standing like stone with thee.
PERDITA
And give me leave,
And do not say ’tis superstition, that
I kneel and then implore her blessing. Lady,
Dear queen, that ended when I but began,
Give me that hand of yours to kiss!
PAULINA
O, patience!
The statue is but newly fixed, the colour’s
Not dry.
CAMILLO
My lord, your sorrow was too sore laid on,
Which sixteen winters cannot blow away,
So many summers dry. Scarce any joy
Did ever so long live; no sorrow
But killed itself much sooner.
POLIXENES
Dear my brother,
Let him that was the cause of this have power
To take off so much grief from you as he
Will piece up in himself.
PAULINA
Indeed, my lord,
If I had thought the sight of my poor image
Would thus have wrought you – for the stone is mine –
I’d not have showed it.
LEONTES
Do not draw the curtain.
PAULINA
No longer shall you gaze on’t, lest your fancy
May think anon it moves.
LEONTES
Let be, let be!
Would I were dead but that methinks already –
What was he that did make it? See, my lord:
Would you not deem it breathed, and that those veins
Did verily bear blood?
POLIXENES
Masterly done!
The very life seems warm upon her lip.
LEONTES
The fixture of her eye has motion in’t
As we are mocked with art.
PAULINA
I’ll draw the curtain.
My lord’s almost so far transported that
He’ll think anon it lives.
LEONTES
O sweet Paulina,
Make me to think so twenty years together!
No settled senses of the world can match
The pleasure of that madness. Let’t alone.
(Act 5, Scene 3)

Question 04
The Winter’s Tale – William Shakespeare
‘The extent of Leontes’ grief completely restores sympathy for him.’
In the light of this view, discuss how Shakespeare presents thoughts and feelings about
Leontes’ past actions in this extract and elsewhere in the play.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Students might consider:
• the view that Leontes’ grief for his past actions concerning Hermione, other family members, close
friends and other courtiers along with Polixenes and his family completely restores sympathy for
him

conveying Hermione’s best personal qualities
• the view that Leontes’ whole demeanour – the respectful way he addresses the statue and
Paulina, as well as references to his own guilt and regret – is an expression of grief
• his conciliatory and respectful attitude towards Paulina
• the references to Leontes’ silence and the emotions that he may be experiencing
• Leontes’ recognition of his own past actions and the necessity for him to be ‘chided’ and ‘rebuked’
• his reluctance for Paulina to draw the curtain and take away the ‘statue’ of Hermione
• the thoughts and feelings of the other characters
• the thoughts and feelings of audiences
• ‘extent’ could refer to the length of time he has endured grief rather than, or as well as, the depth of
grief presented
• the alternative view that it is rather Leontes’ understanding of his own guilt and the need for
penance that restores sympathy
• the view that audiences and/or other characters may not have had sympathy for Leontes in the first
place

restored

• the possible impact of recent debates about the exploitation of women and how their abusers

• etc.

• how attitudes to the following might have changed over time: presentations of grief and sympathy

erText: The Winter’s Tale Extract from Act 5, Scene 3: ‘The extent of Leontes’ grief completely restores sympathy for him.’ In the light of this view, discuss how Shakespeare presents thoughts and feelings about Leontes’ past actions in this extract and elsewhere in the play. What students did well • concentrated on the extract to evaluate sympathy for Leontes in the light of his past words and actions, the views of Paulina and the others present. • allowed for sympathy to include audiences, the other characters in the play and particularly those on stage here. • saw the scene as a prelude to the play’s climax with Leontes noting the lifelike aspects of the statue. • appreciated Paulina’s role in challenging Leontes, perhaps defying the expectations of women at the time. • looked beyond Leontes vs Paulina to consider the roles of Perdita, Polixenes and Camillo. • considered the relevant impact of staging and proxemics. • understood the holistic structure of the play as tragi-comedy/romance and the arc of development towards a conclusion. Common misunderstandings • neglected ‘completely’ as a prompt to debate. • gave narrative accounts of before and after this scene.

text:
Answer the following question.
‘Both speakers blame their own strong feelings for the pain of failed love.’
In the light of this view, compare and contrast the presentation of the pain of failed love in
the following poems.
[25 marks]
I Am No Good at Love
I am no good at love
My heart should be wise and free
I kill the unfortunate golden goose
Whoever it may be
With over-articulate tenderness
And too much intensity.
I am no good at love
I batter it out of shape
Suspicion tears at my sleepless mind
And, gibbering like an ape,
I lie alone in the endless dark
Knowing there’s no escape.
I am no good at love
When my easy heart I yield
Wild words come tumbling from my mouth
Which should have stayed concealed;
And my jealousy turns a bed of bliss
Into a battlefield.
I am no good at love
I betray it with little sins
For I feel the misery of the end
In the moment that it begins
And the bitterness of the last good-bye
Is the bitterness that wins.
Noël Coward (1899–1973)
Never Give All The Heart
Never give all the heart, for love
Will hardly seem worth thinking of
To passionate women if it seem
Certain, and they never dream
That it fades out from kiss to kiss;
For everything that’s lovely is
But a brief, dreamy, kind delight.
O never give the heart outright,
For they, for all smooth lips can say,
Have given their hearts up to the play.
And who could play it well enough
If deaf and dumb and blind with love?
He that made this knows all the cost,
For he gave all his heart and lost.
WB Yeats (1865–1939)
msText:
Question 05
‘Both speakers blame their own strong feelings for the pain of failed love.’
In the light of this view, compare and contrast the presentation of the pain of failed love in
the following poems.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Students might consider:
• the view that the pain of failed love is entirely the fault of the speakers
• the self-destructive nature of both speakers
• the pathos created by the use of first-person
• the ways in which both speakers warn of the pain of over-commitment to love affairs that remain
unrequited or unsatisfied in some way
• the extent of the pain felt, particularly as expressed by the endings of the poems
• the view that Coward’s speaker blames himself for a series of failed relationships; he presents
himself as misguidedly over-enthusiastic leading to awkward and painful abandonment
• the fact that Yeats’ speaker twice warns the reader to ‘never’ give ‘all’ the heart – again, implying
more than one bad experience
• the alternative view that Yeats focuses more on the ‘passionate women’ who prove unreliable (not
liking love that is too ‘certain’, or not accepting that love can fade, or judge lovers by performative
expectations)
• the idea that with Coward’s speaker it is more than ‘generosity of heart’ that is the problem – more
to do with saying too much, being too intense, being suspicious and jealous, being too pessimistic
and bitter, etc
• the self-deprecating comedy of Coward’s speaker and the ways in which he presents his
misadventures in love
• the use of direct address to warn readers of the dangers of commitment
• the use of ‘speakers’, ‘blame’, ‘strong feelings’, ‘pain’, ‘failed love’ in the given view
• the use of lyric and loose sonnet forms to express unhappiness with failed love
• etc.
AO4 Explore connections across literary texts
Focus might be on (in the literature of love):
• representations of: the pain of failed love, either temporary or final; those involved; the
circumstances and effects
• the use of speakers and their accounts of the pain of failed love
• the typicality of these poems as examples of a literary sub-genre of self-deprecation
• the use of anti-heroic tropes that echo the Courtly Love tradition
• uses of lyric and sonnet form
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• the historical contexts of the poems and how attitudes to relationships and the pain of failed love
might have changed over time
• Coward’s use of lyric form
• Coward’s use of anti-heroic tropes that echo the Courtly Love tradition
• Yeats’ use of sonnet form
• poems about failed relationships as a literary sub-genre
• etc.
AO2 Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in literary texts
Focus might be on:
• the contrasting forms of the poems: Coward’s use of the lyric vs Yeats’ use of loose sonnet with
foreshortened lines
• structural issues relating to the forms adopted: Coward’s use of four sestet stanzas, each
expanding upon ‘I am no good at love’, each exploring an abstract concept as a constituent part of
failed love (tenderness, suspicion, jealousy and betrayal) and each arranged around triple rhyme
starting on the second line; Yeats’ use of a loose sonnet with foreshortened lines and a simple
scheme of rhymed/near-rhymed couplets which breaks down into two sections, each exploring the
warning to ‘never give all the heart’ and each focusing on the narrator’s vulnerability when faced
with ‘passionate women’ who are either put off certainty in a world of change or who judge on the
basis of the lover’s performance; both poems end on a note of deeply-felt hurt
• the ways in which both poets use metonymy in the use of the heart to represent passionate
expressions of love
• the confessional nature of both poems and how this affects the poetic methods employed
• the ways in which end-stopped lines, enjambement and caesurae are used as structural devices
within the poems
• the ways in which verse form reflects the feelings and intentions of the narrators
• the ways in which the feelings and intentions of the speakers are reflected in: word choices;
different sentence types
• the ways in which the elliptical nature of poetry raises questions about the narrators and the
relationships to which they allude
• Coward’s speaker’s emphasis on words and the manner of speaking, particularly in the first three
stanzas – ‘gibbering like an ape’, etc
• his use of honest, straightforward language
• his self-deprecating almost comic tone
• his allusion to the fairy tale of the golden goose
• his use of dynamic verbs to suggest his self-destructive tendencies
• his use of the first person to suggest introspective analysis
• metaphors such as ‘bed of bliss’ and ‘battlefield’ to evoke scenes/states in a love affair
• Yeats’ narrator’s more elliptical and ambiguous exposition of the pain of failed love
• the link between ‘passionate women’ and ‘they’
• the use of direct address to the reader, warning of the pain of failed love
• the ways in which ‘the heart’ also suggests a sense of detachment
• the ways in which he describes himself in the third person in the final couplet
• the use of irony
• etc.
AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression
• quality of argument
• organisation of ideas
• use of appropriate concepts and terminology
• technical accuracy
• comparing texts.
Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of
authorial methods.
erText: ‘I Am No Good at Love’ by Noel Coward and ‘Never Give All The Heart’ by W.B. Yeats ‘Both speakers blame their own strong feelings for the pain of failed love.’ In the light of this view, compare and contrast the presentation of the pain of failed love in the following poems. What students did well • readily engaged with the pain of failed love in both poems and addressed the issue of blame. • distinguished between Coward’s speaker’s self-blame and Yeats’ speaker’s blaming of ‘passionate women’. • explored the idea in both poems that love is a game best played by the other party. • unpicked the warning tone, perhaps particularly evident in Yeats’ poem. • compared the endings as summary statements of loss and devastation. • analysed language in support of the feelings identified. • considered the lyric form of Coward vs the subverted sonnet form of Yeats and how both contributed to meaning. Common misunderstandings • asserted that both poems were post-modern, assuming that ‘post-modern’ is a label of time rather than a stylistic choice. • neglected the issue of blame. • conflated the writer and the speaker in an assertive fashion. • identified poetic methods without linking them relevantly to meaning. • labelled the rhyme scheme(s) incorrectly. • labelled Yeats’ sonnet form incorrectly, often as Shakespearean. • neglected form and structure as methods to analyse. • missed the hyperbolic humour of Coward, overly characterising the speaker as embittered and despairing. • wrote narrative/descriptive commentary with embedded quotations as a substitute for analysis. • concentrated on Coward as the perceived easier option. • made assertions about context with little or no evidence, eg about Coward’s experience in WW1 and WW2, and about Yeats being a Victorian with typically Victorian attitudes.

Question 01
Up the Line to Death – ed. Brian Gardner
‘The most powerful poems focus on passive endurance rather than active combat.’
Examine this view of the anthology.
You must write about at least two poems in your answer.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Students might consider:
• later poems such as Owen’s ‘Exposure’ which focus on the passive endurance of soldiers and the
harsh conditions of the front line
• poems that focus on the passive, inactive nature of trench warfare; for example, Nichol’s ‘Noon’
and Sassoon’s ‘The Dugout’
• poems such as Aldington’s ‘Bombardment’ and Owen’s ‘The Sentry’ which present the passive
suffering endured during prolonged bombardment
• the extent to which many poems consider the anticipation and aftermath of action, but rarely active
combat itself
• poems which celebrate active combat in heroic terms such as Seeger’s ‘The Aisne’
• poems such as Grenfell’s ‘Into Battle’ that focus on the exhilaration of active combat that seems
part of a natural order
• poems such as Sassoon’s ‘Attack’ which present the chaos and suffering of active combat
• varying approaches to ‘powerful poems’; for example, through a consideration of powerful poetic
effects such as voice and diction, or a poem’s impact in the anthology as a whole
• the keywords ‘passive’, ‘active combat’, ‘endurance’ and ‘powerful’ in the given view
• etc.
AO4 Explore connections across literary texts
Focus might be on:
• typical representations of trench warfare in the literature of WW1 and its aftermath
• the typical presentation of the varying emotions and attitudes associated with passive endurance
and more active combat
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• how poems written early in the war might idealise the active nature of combat
• the structuring of the anthology by Gardner
• the differing poetic approaches to the presentation of combat and the reality of trench warfare
• the war experience of individual poets and the differing perspectives they offer
• etc.
AO2 Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in literary texts
Focus might be on:
• aspects of poetic form and genre
• aspects of structure, eg use of stanzas
• aspects of language, eg rhyme, rhythm, imagery
• the organisation of the anthology
• etc.
AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression
• quality of argument
• organisation of ideas
• use of appropriate concepts and terminology
• technical accuracy.
Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of
authorial methods.
erText: Better answers: • engaged purposefully with the keywords ‘powerful’, ‘passive endurance’ and ‘active combat’ • considered the context of time relevantly though considering how later war poetry often focused more powerfully on ‘passive endurance’ • purposefully considered ‘powerful poetry’ through well selected analysis of poetic methods • fully debated and challenged the given view through considering varying ways in which ‘active combat’ is presented • demonstrated an accurate understanding of Gardner’s selection and organisation of the anthology. Less effective answers: • only had a superficial grasp of the keywords of the given view and tended to resort to pre-planned material that compared early and post-Somme poetry a broad way • did not select appropriate poems and often over-relied on predictable, heavily rehearsed readings of Dulce et Decorum Est • tended to unload comments on poetic methods rather than considering how these techniques shape meaning • used context in a generalised way rather than using it as a relevant literary tool to explore meaning.

AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations

• how women are pressured to accept male authority through the political and religious responses to
war
• the forms of female dissent against a war controlled by men
• etc.

• the forms of female dissent against male authority
• etc.

• aspects of poetic form and genre

• aspects of language, eg rhyme, rhythm, imagery

• etc.

Less effective answers: • produced ‘context heavy’ responses that considered the changing roles of women during the war and could only focus on some textual details as a form of cross- reference • made poor poem selections because of an insecure grasp of the whole anthology • did not engage with all the keywords of the given view and were unable to set up a convincing agenda from the start • over-relied on familiar, well-taught poems which were not always relevant to the task.

msText:
Question 05
Explore the significance of team spirit and shared values in this extract.
Remember to include in your answer relevant detailed analysis of the ways that Harris shapes
meanings.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Focus might be on:
•
‘team spirit’ and ‘shared values’ equally or one might be prioritised
•
Harris’s presentation of the shared patriotic triggers that create a team spirit; the performance
of the ‘sceptred isle’ speech and the singing of the national anthem
•
Harris’s presentation of Fenner as a typical volunteer soldier from 1914 still imbued with the
team spirit and shared values shown at the start of the war
•
how the sense of team spirit and shared values is a recognition that the forthcoming battle will
be the culmination of Fenner’s two years of military experience and training with his comrades
•
the shared values of personal and national destiny
•
the presentation of team spirit as an underlying quality that unifies the men, not just an aspect
of military life
•
the unreal, almost religious presentation of the shared values of nationalism amongst the
troops; the belief that they were ‘the chosen people’
•
the collective team spirit to die in a battle that would be a ‘holocaust that would end the war’
•
the dream-like, deluded emotions that are part of patriotic shared values; ‘the tendency to be
tolerant with the sentimental, even with the would-be heroic, was strong’
•
one or both of the key phrases ‘team spirit’ and ‘shared values’
•
etc.
AO4 Explore connections across literary texts
Focus might be on:
• typical presentations of team spirit and shared values in texts about the war
• the ways in which team spirit and shared values are typically presented through patriotism,
comradeship and esprit de corps
• typical presentations of shared, positive values reinforced before combat
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• differing attitudes to the shared values present in positive military morale such as team spirit/esprit
de corps and patriotism over time
• differing attitudes over time to the team spirit and shared values of volunteer soldiers and pals’
battalions
• differing attitudes towards the team spirit and the shared patriotic values that might lead soldiers to
feel that their part in the war is justified
• differing attitudes towards military pride and preparation and the team spirit and shared values
shown in the collective act of preparing for a ‘Big Push’
• etc.
AO2 Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in literary texts
Focus might be on:
• the use of listing and repetitive use of definite articles in the first paragraph to stress the scale of
the collective preparation for ‘The Big Push’
• how the preparations for the attack have unified the men; the use of listing ‘the heroes, the
cowards, the fainthearts and the strong together’ presents that the planned attack is above
individual strengths and weaknesses
• the string of animalistic similes to present war as something beyond the human; for example, the
bombardment as ‘like the flutterings of gigantic wings’, ‘like some iron monster’, ‘like some
tremendous beast about to spring’
• the extra-textual use of the speech from Richard II to set the moment in a literary and patriotic
context
• the triplet of adjectives ‘firm, sincere, young’ to present the power of Murray’s delivery of the
Shakespeare speech; the use of Murray’s character to denote the patriotism of young volunteer
soldiers
• the repeated use of singular and plural first-person pronouns throughout the passage
• the first-person narrative and indirect discourse that is measured, yet emotive; for example through
the triplet of adjectives, ‘I felt proud and sad, and glad I was there’
• the personification of death, ‘Death wasn’t very far away over the hill that night’
• the use of spatial metaphors to denote an awareness of destiny, ‘poised on a lofty height’
• the biblical language used to present the almost religious patriotic spirit of the troops ‘we were the
chosen people’
• etc.
AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression
• quality of argument
• organisation of ideas
• use of appropriate concepts and terminology
• technical accuracy.
Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of
authorial methods.
erText: The unseen extract was selected to allow students to fully engage with prose methods. The extract was deliberately accessible in terms of length; well prepared students would have time to read, reread and plan before writing. This question always requires students to engage in ‘relevant detailed analysis’ as a way of discussing how the writer shapes meaning when considering the keywords of the given view which in this series was team spirit and shared values. Clear focus on the given view allows students to structure a reading that doesn’t just ‘go through’ the extract with paraphrase and list-like analysis of prose methods. Full engagement with the given view encourages a more selective, thorough approach that allows the student to draw together literary analysis and contextual knowledge in a cohesive way. Successful students clearly benefit from exam practice that builds effective time management through focused reading and planning. Careful reading of the question and the preamble is crucial. Reading the preamble helps the student consider the context of the time of setting and publication. Examiners noted that many students grasped the significance of a writer born in 1916 growing up in the inter-war years and who had adult experience of the second World War. Students alert to the 1961 publication date were able to consider the literary context and the revisionary approach to a war that allowed for the massive casualties experienced during the Battle of the Somme. Careful reading of the preamble also allowed students to consider the men who ‘volunteered’ together in pals divisions and the impact of mass casualties on their communities. The best work always considered ‘team spirit’ and ‘shared values’ precisely and did not conflate the two. ‘Team spirit’ was explored through considering rhetorical patterns that stressed the collective nature of the immense preparation for battle through repetition of number and adjectives. Repetition of clauses and listing was seen to reinforce the collective nature of ‘team spirit’. Many confident students considered ‘shared values’ to underpin the military discipline of ‘team spirit’ and discussed the presentation of patriotism and national pride in the extract. The use of the Richard II speech allowed students to consider pastoral, spiritual imagery that they thought was typical of early war sentiments. Some sophisticated responses considered the biblical echoes of the narrator’s sense that they were ‘the chosen people, poised on a lofty height’. The singing of ‘God Save the King’ was carefully considered; many could comment on the significance of collective act of singing, others considered how important the anthem was an act of patriotism and how engrained it was in Edwardian England. Less able students tended to treat the text in isolation and were unable to consider many of the contextual prompts highlighted in the preamble. More assertive responses engaged with the given view through criticising the naïve patriotic attitudes of the author. Some students recognised the 1960s context of publication and felt that the patriotism presented in the extract was atypical of the time. More successful students confidently considered narrative form and recognised the irony and pathos embedded in the presentation of ‘team spirit’ and ‘shared values’ before the historical tragedy of The Battle of the Somme. This work carefully considered the significance of the retrospective first person narrative and explored the imagery with more subtlety. These responses explored how ‘team spirt’ was merely subsumed into a vast mechanised war that was represented through the simile of the ‘iron monster’. Less able students misread the imagery and concluded that this was the force that the soldiers would need to fight against. More assured students recognised that this was ‘The Big Push’ that had been promised as an offensive that would win the war. Confident students explored the true nature of ‘team spirit’ through focusing on specific verb choices; men were mere commodities that would be ‘snatched’ and ‘flung’ into ‘the final holocaust’. Again, the most sophisticated responses explored the religious notion of ‘holocaust’ and sensibly considered the extract in the wider context of the novel’s title, Covenant with Death. More successful extract-based answers • always explored the extract through considering the significance of ‘team spirit and shared values’ • never treated the extract in isolation; had a secure overview of prose structure and perspective as well as using varying contexts to consider the significance of team spirit and shared values’ • did not see prose methods as a simple check list, but through engaging with ‘significance’ purposely considered how the writer shaped meaning. Textual detail was chosen carefully and analysis served to develop an argument rather than as an end in itself • integrated contextual knowledge into the argument rather than using it as an add-on. Always considered the extract and the topic within the shared context of the option • communicated with clarity with an appropriate literary register. Less successful extract-based answers • frequently lost sight of the significance of ‘team spirit and shared values’ and ‘went through’ the extract in a decontextualised way noting prose methods without considering how they shape meaning • either treated the text in isolation, or discussed context in a digressive way which led the student away from the extract • tended to ‘feature spot’ prose methods and sometimes produced over-elaborate readings based on the use of punctuation or misapplied poetic terminology such as ‘volta’ to a prose text • did not read carefully and produced misreadings to support over-assertive ideas • did not communicate clearly and sometimes adopted an over-elaborated style of writing perhaps to create an academic register. Students need to be reminded that the best work communicates complex ideas simply.

erText: In Paper 1, two out of three tasks involve explicit comparison. In Papers 2A and 2B, one out of three tasks is explicitly comparative. The NEA task is also explicitly comparative. In stark contrast, Specification B never asks students to compare one text with another. There are other kinds of comparison involved in Specification A tasks too, of course, such as explicit or implicit comparison within the shared contexts to establish typicality or atypicality. A clear understanding of the task was key to success in this comparative element of section B. Students were asked to compare the significance of team spirit and shared values across two texts from different genres. Well-prepared students clearly familiar with the unchanging format of this task. Successful comparisons explored differences, not just similarities. They considered how the given theme was presented in both texts, focusing on the differing genres and literary methods. Weaker responses relied on content similarities and narrative paraphrasing, ignoring genre differences. Understanding 'significance' is crucial for considering genres, methods, and contexts that create meaning. Successful students used precise literary language appropriate to poetry, drama, and prose. Less successful work often focused on word-level analysis and misapplied poetic terms to drama and prose. Work that was less successful tended to focus more on demonstrating knowledge and understanding of the chosen texts, rather than selecting material relevant to 'team spirit and shared values'. These efforts often involved treating the two texts separately through extensive sections on each individual text, using brief discourse markers such as 'similarly' or 'on the other hand'. In contrast, more thoughtful work seamlessly integrated discussions of both texts and purposefully analysed well-chosen textual details to construct a convincing comparison. To achieve higher marks, students should establish comparative links by thoughtfully and precisely selecting textual details, rather than attempting to demonstrate familiarity with their texts through narrative-driven work that may become digressive. The chosen theme of ‘team spirit and shared values’ was accessible to the majority of students. Importantly, many students produced responses that focused on how ‘team spirit and shared values’ differed and could became a source of conflict. Such work considered conflict within the military hierarchy where ‘team spirit and shared values’ were often very different. The dramatic conflict between Hibbert and Stanhope in Journey’s End was often purposefully considered as Sherriff’s way of presenting the necessity of ‘team spirit’ on the front-line. In The Wipers Times ‘shared values’ was often explored through considering the conflict between Roberts and the military hierarchy represented by Howfield who opposes the newspaper and states that ‘The battlefield is not the place for humour’. Students also compared how presentations of ‘team spirit and shared values’ differ because of time. These responses purposely compared early and later war poetry through a comparison with characters such as Raleigh or Stanhope from Journey’s End, or Burns and Sassoon from Regeneration. Students also successfully compared the differing presentations of home-front and front-line values. Such work considered the ’team spirit’ presented in Jessie Pope’s poetry or the lack of ‘shared values’ that soldiers experience when they are away from the front-line in Regeneration or Birdsong. Successful work shows that understanding different contexts can help explore meaning in a precise and nuanced way. However, many students discuss context in a way that becomes digressive and moves away from close textual analysis. For instance, discussing ‘the shared values’ represented in propaganda and jingoism should be integrated into an analysis of the characterisation of Howfield in The Wipers Times or Hamilton’s poem The Jingo-Woman. Less successful students often focused on individual words rather than considering form and structure. This led to assertive interpretations based on sometimes inaccurate linguistic analysis. In this work there was also a tendency to misapply poetic analysis to other genres. AQA’s Teaching Guide to AO2 offers a better method for understanding how meaning is constructed across genres. https://www.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/as-and-a-level/english-literature-a/teach/teaching-guide-ao2 More successful comparative set text answers: • consider the given view through comparing the two chosen texts • move fluently between texts often exploring difference rather than just similarity • carefully select relevant textual details to support ideas • have a secure understanding of poetic, dramatic and/or prose methods • always link literary analysis to meaning • integrate an understanding of context into literary analysis • can consider how texts may shape meaning in a more tentative fashion when necessary • show awareness of typicality in the literature of WW1 and its aftermath. Less successful comparative set text answers: • lose sight of the given topic and resort to narrative paraphrase • tend to unload ideas often leading to digressive work which can be rushed and incomplete • tend to be assertive and are not supported by well-chosen references • can only ‘feature spot’ sometimes inaccurately and can only link methods to meaning in an assertive unconvincing way • make generalised references to context and typicality that lead to assertive, inaccurate arguments. Secure AO1 is essential when comparing two texts using a central argument. Students who effectively used these AO1 tools often gave more successful responses: • clear introductions and conclusions that focus on the keywords and frame the response • clear paragraphing to build structured comparison • purposeful discourse markers to highlight comparative thinking • clear succinct expression that avoids imprecise, overlong sentences • clear use of topic sentences to guide a purposeful argument. still took the opportunity to use My Boy Jack as they were able to compare the text with the post-2000 novels A Long Long Way or Life Class. Those who chose The Wipers Times as the post-2000 text could chose texts such as Regeneration, All Quiet on the Western Front or Birdsong. Many students purposefully compared the ‘shared values’ of the home-front and the front-line. Through precise consideration of Sassoon’s characterisation in Regeneration, students were able to explore the conflict between protesting against the conduct of the war and his duty towards his men.

In the light of this view, examine the presentation of Osborne in Journey’s End.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Students might consider:
• different interpretations of the role of ‘the teacher’; the differing roles associated with teaching such
as mentorship, leadership, pastoral support and discipline, etc
• Osborne’s position in the group is an extension of his past role as teacher; he is the protective
‘uncle’ who cares for Stanhope and guides Raleigh when he arrives
• how he establishes the debate about Stanhope’s worth as a leader when speaking to Hardy at the
start of the play
• how Osborne represents the key qualities of an older officer through his loyalty, care and
diplomacy
• he is a pivotal character; the audience often learns about other characters through his observations
and interactions
• his reflective character allows for the presentation of the strangeness of war; for example, his
observation to Raleigh that there is something ‘romantic’ about the front line
• the impact of his death on the group of officers
• the significance of his role as an older officer who is seen as a supportive ‘Uncle’ figure
• the significance of public-school education
• alternative views that Osborne is defined by other roles; eg as a professional soldier
• the possible impact of particular production(s) on the interpretation of the question
• etc.
AO4 Explore connections across literary texts
Focus might be on:
• the differing ways that WW1 Literature focuses on the roles and duties of officers
• relationships between officers on the front line
• the presentation of older officers
• friendships between older and younger men
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• the changing attitudes to the role of a teacher over time and across the class divide; for example
the public school perception of leadership and loyalty engendered by teachers might be different to
the experience of teachers shared by Trotter and Mason
• the experience of the front-line officer in WW1
• the changing views on the roles, attitudes, and values of front-line officers
• the changing views on authority and duty
• the significance of male perspectives in a play written by a man for an all male cast
• etc.
AO2 Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in literary texts
Focus might be on:
• the use of dialogue to convey the interactions between officers on the front line
• the importance of props such as Osborne’s bed and the personal effects that Osborne leaves with
Stanhope before the trench raid
• the shared language of school and sport
• Osborne’s repeated reference to Alice in Wonderland and the part it plays in the presentation of
war
• the privileging of Osborne’s perspective within in the play; for example, his views on Stanhope
when arguing with Hardy and his talk with Raleigh when he arrives
• his presence in climactic scenes such as Act 2 Scene 2 when he reads Raleigh’s letter out loud
• etc.
AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression
• quality of argument
• organisation of ideas
• use of appropriate concepts and terminology
• technical accuracy.
Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of

erText: Better answers: • engaged with the given view to develop a focused discussion on Osborne's presentation by considering his authority and interactions with other characters. • were able to consider his dramatic function within the play and discuss how he is used to present Stanhope through his interactions with Hardy and Raleigh • purposefully debated the view through considering his relationships with Raleigh and Stanhope • used contextual knowledge of public-school culture to consider Osborne and his relationships with the other men • confidently considered the dramatic significance of Osborne’s death through considering props such as Osborne’s bed and the varying reactions to his death. Less effective answers: • treated Osborne as a real person and could not discuss his dramatic presentation • used the given view as a simple essay frame to list Osborne’s qualities as a teacher in a generalised, assertive way • did not consider dramatic methods other than paraphrasing the stage notes on Osborne on the first page of the play • largely ignored the presentation of his death and the repercussions on the other characters • failed to comment on the common public-school background that unites Osborne, Raleigh and Stanhope. • made mistaken assertions that Osborne was a headteacher.

Read the Insert. Answer both questions in this section.
Read the Insert carefully. It is taken from Covenant with Death, a novel by John Harris (1916–1991),
published in 1961. In the extract, Mark Fenner and his friend Murray, who both volunteered to fight in
1914, are part of an unplanned concert before the Battle of the Somme.
Explore the significance of team spirit and shared values in this extract.
Remember to include in your answer relevant detailed analysis of the ways that Harris
shapes meanings.
[25 marks]
msText:
Question 11
Explore the significance of team spirit and shared values in this extract.
Remember to include in your answer relevant detailed analysis of the ways that Harris shapes
meanings.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Focus might be on:
•
team spirit’ and ‘shared values’ equally or one might be prioritised
•
Harris’s presentation of the shared patriotic triggers that create a team spirit; the performance
of the ‘sceptred isle’ speech and the singing of the national anthem
•
Harris’s presentation of Fenner as a typical volunteer soldier from 1914 still imbued with the
team spirit and shared values shown at the start of the war
•
how the sense of team spirit and shared values is a recognition that the forthcoming battle will
be the culmination of Fenner’s two years of military experience and training with his comrades
•
the shared values of personal and national destiny
•
the presentation of team spirit as an underlying quality that unifies the men, not just an aspect
of military life
•
the unreal, almost religious presentation of the shared values of nationalism amongst the
troops; the belief that they were ‘the chosen people’
•
the collective team spirit to die in a battle that would be a ‘holocaust that would end the war’
•
the dream-like, deluded emotions that are part of patriotic shared values; ‘the tendency to be
tolerant with the sentimental, even with the would-be heroic, was strong’
•
one or both of the key phrases ‘team spirit’ and ‘shared values’
•
etc.
AO4 Explore connections across literary texts
Focus might be on:
• typical presentations of team spirit and shared values in texts about the war
• the ways in which team spirit and shared values are typically presented through patriotism,
comradeship and esprit de corps
• typical presentations of shared, positive values reinforced before combat
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• differing attitudes to the shared values present in positive military morale such as team spirit/esprit
de corps and patriotism over time
• differing attitudes over time to the team spirit and shared values of volunteer soldiers and pals’
battalions
• differing attitudes towards the team spirit and the shared patriotic values that might lead soldiers to
feel that their part in the war is justified
• differing attitudes towards military pride and preparation and the team spirit and shared values
shown in the collective act of preparing for a ‘Big Push’
• etc.
AO2 Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in literary texts
Focus might be on:
• the use of listing and repetitive use of definite articles in the first paragraph to stress the scale of
the collective preparation for ‘The Big Push’
• how the preparations for the attack have unified the men; the use of listing ‘the heroes, the
cowards, the fainthearts and the strong together’ presents that the planned attack is above
individual strengths and weaknesses
• the string of animalistic similes to present war as something beyond the human; for example, the
bombardment as ‘like the flutterings of gigantic wings’, ‘like some iron monster’, ‘like some
tremendous beast about to spring’
• the extra-textual use of the speech from Richard II to set the moment in a literary and patriotic
context
• the triplet of adjectives ‘firm, sincere, young’ to present the power of Murray’s delivery of the
Shakespeare speech; the use of Murray’s character to denote the patriotism of young volunteer
soldiers
• the repeated use of singular and plural first-person pronouns throughout the passage
• the first-person narrative and indirect discourse that is measured, yet emotive; for example through
the triplet of adjectives, ‘I felt proud and sad, and glad I was there’
• the personification of death, ‘Death wasn’t very far away over the hill that night’
• the use of spatial metaphors to denote an awareness of destiny, ‘poised on a lofty height’
• the biblical language used to present the almost religious patriotic spirit of the troops ‘we were the
chosen people’
• etc.
AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression
• quality of argument
• organisation of ideas
• use of appropriate concepts and terminology
• technical accuracy.
Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of
authorial methods.
erText: The unseen extract was selected to allow students to fully engage with prose methods. The extract was deliberately accessible in terms of length; well prepared students would have time to read, reread and plan before writing. This question always requires students to engage in ‘relevant detailed analysis’ as a way of discussing how the writer shapes meaning when considering the keywords of the given view which in this series was team spirit and shared values. Clear focus on the given view allows students to structure a reading that doesn’t just ‘go through’ the extract with paraphrase and list-like analysis of prose methods. Full engagement with the given view encourages a more selective, thorough approach that allows the student to draw together literary analysis and contextual knowledge in a cohesive way. Successful students clearly benefit from exam practice that builds effective time management through focused reading and planning. Careful reading of the question and the preamble is crucial. Reading the preamble helps the student consider the context of the time of setting and publication. Examiners noted that many students grasped the significance of a writer born in 1916 growing up in the inter-war years and who had adult experience of the second World War. Students alert to the 1961 publication date were able to consider the literary context and the revisionary approach to a war that allowed for the massive casualties experienced during the Battle of the Somme. Careful reading of the preamble also allowed students to consider the men who ‘volunteered’ together in pals divisions and the impact of mass casualties on their communities. The best work always considered ‘team spirit’ and ‘shared values’ precisely and did not conflate the two. ‘Team spirit’ was explored through considering rhetorical patterns that stressed the collective nature of the immense preparation for battle through repetition of number and adjectives. Repetition of clauses and listing was seen to reinforce the collective nature of ‘team spirit’. Many confident students considered ‘shared values’ to underpin the military discipline of ‘team spirit’ and discussed the presentation of patriotism and national pride in the extract. The use of the Richard II speech allowed students to consider pastoral, spiritual imagery that they thought was typical of early war sentiments. Some sophisticated responses considered the biblical echoes of the narrator’s sense that they were ‘the chosen people, poised on a lofty height’. The singing of ‘God Save the King’ was carefully considered; many could comment on the significance of collective act of singing, others considered how important the anthem was an act of patriotism and how engrained it was in Edwardian England. Less able students tended to treat the text in isolation and were unable to consider many of the contextual prompts highlighted in the preamble. More assertive responses engaged with the given view through criticising the naïve patriotic attitudes of the author. Some students recognised the 1960s context of publication and felt that the patriotism presented in the extract was atypical of the time. More successful students confidently considered narrative form and recognised the irony and pathos embedded in the presentation of ‘team spirit’ and ‘shared values’ before the historical tragedy of The Battle of the Somme. This work carefully considered the significance of the retrospective first person narrative and explored the imagery with more subtlety. These responses explored how ‘team spirt’ was merely subsumed into a vast mechanised war that was represented through the simile of the ‘iron monster’. Less able students misread the imagery and concluded that this was the force that the soldiers would need to fight against. More assured students recognised that this was ‘The Big Push’ that had been promised as an offensive that would win the war. Confident students explored the true nature of ‘team spirit’ through focusing on specific verb choices; men were mere commodities that would be ‘snatched’ and ‘flung’ into ‘the final holocaust’. Again, the most sophisticated responses explored the religious notion of ‘holocaust’ and sensibly considered the extract in the wider context of the novel’s title, Covenant with Death. More successful extract-based answers • always explored the extract through considering the significance of ‘team spirit and shared values’ • never treated the extract in isolation; had a secure overview of prose structure and perspective as well as using varying contexts to consider the significance of team spirit and shared values’ • did not see prose methods as a simple check list, but through engaging with ‘significance’ purposely considered how the writer shaped meaning. Textual detail was chosen carefully and analysis served to develop an argument rather than as an end in itself • integrated contextual knowledge into the argument rather than using it as an add-on. Always considered the extract and the topic within the shared context of the option • communicated with clarity with an appropriate literary register. Less successful extract-based answers • frequently lost sight of the significance of ‘team spirit and shared values’ and ‘went through’ the extract in a decontextualised way noting prose methods without considering how they shape meaning • either treated the text in isolation, or discussed context in a digressive way which led the student away from the extract • tended to ‘feature spot’ prose methods and sometimes produced over-elaborate readings based on the use of punctuation or misapplied poetic terminology such as ‘volta’ to a prose text • did not read carefully and produced misreadings to support over-assertive ideas • did not communicate clearly and sometimes adopted an over-elaborated style of writing perhaps to create an academic register. Students need to be reminded that the best work communicates complex ideas simply.

Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Focus might be on:

• the debate around team spirit and shared values through the consideration of ideas and attitudes
such as military morale, patriotism and group loyalty as presented in their two texts

Focus might be on:

• dramatic methods such as: explicit structural devices; dramatic irony; stage directions; indirect
ways of communicating the writers’ messages and ideas; naturalistic and other styles of

for rhetorical effect; use of aural devices for rhetorical effect; elliptical use of language

AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression
• quality of argument
• organisation of ideas
• use of appropriate concepts and terminology
• technical accuracy
• comparing texts.
Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of
authorial methods.
erText: In Paper 1, two out of three tasks involve explicit comparison. In Papers 2A and 2B, one out of three tasks is explicitly comparative. The NEA task is also explicitly comparative. In stark contrast, Specification B never asks students to compare one text with another. There are other kinds of comparison involved in Specification A tasks too, of course, such as explicit or implicit comparison within the shared contexts to establish typicality or atypicality. A clear understanding of the task was key to success in this comparative element of section B. Students were asked to compare the significance of team spirit and shared values across two texts from different genres. Well-prepared students clearly familiar with the unchanging format of this task. Successful comparisons explored differences, not just similarities. They considered how the given theme was presented in both texts, focusing on the differing genres and literary methods. Weaker responses relied on content similarities and narrative paraphrasing, ignoring genre differences. Understanding 'significance' is crucial for considering genres, methods, and contexts that create meaning. Successful students used precise literary language appropriate to poetry, drama, and prose. Less successful work often focused on word-level analysis and misapplied poetic terms to drama and prose. Work that was less successful tended to focus more on demonstrating knowledge and understanding of the chosen texts, rather than selecting material relevant to 'team spirit and shared values'. These efforts often involved treating the two texts separately through extensive sections on each individual text, using brief discourse markers such as 'similarly' or 'on the other hand'. In contrast, more thoughtful work seamlessly integrated discussions of both texts and purposefully analysed well-chosen textual details to construct a convincing comparison. To achieve higher marks, students should establish comparative links by thoughtfully and precisely selecting textual details, rather than attempting to demonstrate familiarity with their texts through narrative-driven work that may become digressive. The chosen theme of ‘team spirit and shared values’ was accessible to the majority of students. Importantly, many students produced responses that focused on how ‘team spirit and shared values’ differed and could became a source of conflict. Such work considered conflict within the military hierarchy where ‘team spirit and shared values’ were often very different. The dramatic conflict between Hibbert and Stanhope in Journey’s End was often purposefully considered as Sherriff’s way of presenting the necessity of ‘team spirit’ on the front-line. In The Wipers Times ‘shared values’ was often explored through considering the conflict between Roberts and the military hierarchy represented by Howfield who opposes the newspaper and states that ‘The battlefield is not the place for humour’. Students also compared how presentations of ‘team spirit and shared values’ differ because of time. These responses purposely compared early and later war poetry through a comparison with characters such as Raleigh or Stanhope from Journey’s End, or Burns and Sassoon from Regeneration. Students also successfully compared the differing presentations of home-front and front-line values. Such work considered the ’team spirit’ presented in Jessie Pope’s poetry or the lack of ‘shared values’ that soldiers experience when they are away from the front-line in Regeneration or Birdsong. Successful work shows that understanding different contexts can help explore meaning in a precise and nuanced way. However, many students discuss context in a way that becomes digressive and moves away from close textual analysis. For instance, discussing ‘the shared values’ represented in propaganda and jingoism should be integrated into an analysis of the characterisation of Howfield in The Wipers Times or Hamilton’s poem The Jingo-Woman. Less successful students often focused on individual words rather than considering form and structure. This led to assertive interpretations based on sometimes inaccurate linguistic analysis. In this work there was also a tendency to misapply poetic analysis to other genres. AQA’s Teaching Guide to AO2 offers a better method for understanding how meaning is constructed across genres. https://www.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/as-and-a-level/english-literature-a/teach/teaching-guide-ao2 More successful comparative set text answers: • consider the given view through comparing the two chosen texts • move fluently between texts often exploring difference rather than just similarity • carefully select relevant textual details to support ideas • have a secure understanding of poetic, dramatic and/or prose methods • always link literary analysis to meaning • integrate an understanding of context into literary analysis • can consider how texts may shape meaning in a more tentative fashion when necessary • show awareness of typicality in the literature of WW1 and its aftermath. Less successful comparative set text answers: • lose sight of the given topic and resort to narrative paraphrase • tend to unload ideas often leading to digressive work which can be rushed and incomplete • tend to be assertive and are not supported by well-chosen references • can only ‘feature spot’ sometimes inaccurately and can only link methods to meaning in an assertive unconvincing way • make generalised references to context and typicality that lead to assertive, inaccurate arguments. Secure AO1 is essential when comparing two texts using a central argument. Students who effectively used these AO1 tools often gave more successful responses: • clear introductions and conclusions that focus on the keywords and frame the response • clear paragraphing to build structured comparison • purposeful discourse markers to highlight comparative thinking • clear succinct expression that avoids imprecise, overlong sentences • clear use of topic sentences to guide a purposeful argument. responses chose precise textual material for focused comparison. For example, students studying Regeneration could examine the theme through the relationship between Sassoon and Rivers or focus on Rivers’ empathetic methods conflicting with military discipline. Relevant poems were aptly linked, and comparisons focused on the presentation of early war versus post-Somme shared values. While ‘Dulce et Decorum Est’ was a popular choice, many students struggled to discuss it relevantly, often relying on pre-prepared content about the horrors of war. Stronger responses examined ‘team spirit’ in the poem by considering both the officer’s actions and his enduring trauma. More sophisticated analyses addressed the second-person narrative and the writer’s intention to challenge pro-war attitudes, reflecting his duty towards the common soldier.

erText: Better answers: • explored significance through considering setting in terms of the physical place, its role as an institution and its literary function in the novel as a whole • considered the use of an historical location to offer a fresh perspective on war experience and trauma away from the front line • were able to consider the physical presentation of Craiglockhart and how it is used to convey the claustrophobic nature of post-traumatic stress • could explore Craiglockhart’s function to present the conflict between military duty and discipline with the more empathetic talking cure employed by Rivers • set an agenda that drew together contextual knowledge of Craiglockhart and historical characters into discussions about the writer’s use of the setting. • demonstrated expert textual knowledge through well-chosen textual evidence supported by relevant analysis of prose methods. Less effective answers: • failed to set an agenda about the significance of the setting at the start of the response • offered a narrative paraphrase of Sassoon’s arrival at Craiglockhart at the start of the novel and then focused on character rather than setting • unloaded contextual knowledge of Craiglockhart, but failed to discuss its function as a literary setting • resorted to pre-planned material based on past questions that focused on characters rather than setting • resorted to narrative paraphrase • confused ‘significance’ with importance • failed to comment on prose methods.

mistakes: Focus: theme: trauma never cured or overcome
