msText:
Question 17
Explore the significance of team spirit and shared values in this extract.
Remember to include in your answer relevant detailed analysis of the ways that Harris shapes
meanings.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Focus might be on:
• team spirit’ and ‘shared values’ equally or one might be prioritised
• Harris’s presentation of the shared patriotic triggers that create a team spirit; the performance of
the ‘sceptred isle’ speech and the singing of the national anthem
• Harris’s presentation of Fenner as a typical volunteer soldier from 1914 still imbued with the team
spirit and shared values shown at the start of the war
• how the sense of team spirit and shared values is a recognition that the forthcoming battle will be
the culmination of Fenner’s two years of military experience and training with his comrades
• the shared values of personal and national destiny
• the presentation of team spirit as an underlying quality that unifies the men, not just an aspect of
military life
• the unreal, almost religious presentation of the shared values of nationalism amongst the troops;
the belief that they were ‘the chosen people’
• the collective team spirit to die in a battle that would be a ‘holocaust that would end the war’
• the dream-like, deluded emotions that are part of patriotic shared values; ‘the tendency to be
tolerant with the sentimental, even with the would-be heroic, was strong’
• one or both of the key phrases ‘team spirit’ and ‘shared values’
• etc.
AO4 Explore connections across literary texts
Focus might be on:
• typical presentations of team spirit and shared values in texts about the war
• the ways in which team spirit and shared values are typically presented through patriotism,
comradeship and esprit de corps
• typical presentations of shared, positive values reinforced before combat
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• differing attitudes to the shared values present in positive military morale such as team spirit/esprit
de corps and patriotism over time
• differing attitudes over time to the team spirit and shared values of volunteer soldiers and pals’
battalions
• differing attitudes towards the team spirit and the shared patriotic values that might lead soldiers to
feel that their part in the war is justified
• differing attitudes towards military pride and preparation and the team spirit and shared values
shown in the collective act of preparing for a ‘Big Push’
• etc.
AO2 Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in literary texts
Focus might be on:
• the use of listing and repetitive use of definite articles in the first paragraph to stress the scale of
the collective preparation for ‘The Big Push’
• how the preparations for the attack have unified the men; the use of listing ‘the heroes, the
cowards, the fainthearts and the strong together’ presents that the planned attack is above
individual strengths and weaknesses
• the string of animalistic similes to present war as something beyond the human; for example, the
bombardment as ‘like the flutterings of gigantic wings’, ‘like some iron monster’, ‘like some
tremendous beast about to spring’
• the extra-textual use of the speech from Richard II to set the moment in a literary and patriotic
context
• the triplet of adjectives ‘firm, sincere, young’ to present the power of Murray’s delivery of the
Shakespeare speech; the use of Murray’s character to denote the patriotism of young volunteer
soldiers
• the repeated use of singular and plural first-person pronouns throughout the passage
• the first-person narrative and indirect discourse that is measured, yet emotive; for example,
through the triplet of adjectives, ‘I felt proud and sad, and glad I was there’
• the personification of death, ‘Death wasn’t very far away over the hill that night’
• the use of spatial metaphors to denote an awareness of destiny, ‘poised on a lofty height’
• the biblical language used to present the almost religious patriotic spirit of the troops ‘we were the
chosen people’
• etc.
AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression
• quality of argument
• organisation of ideas
• use of appropriate concepts and terminology
• technical accuracy.
Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of
authorial methods.
erText: The unseen extract was selected to allow students to fully engage with prose methods. The extract was deliberately accessible in terms of length; well prepared students would have time to read, reread and plan before writing. This question always requires students to engage in ‘relevant detailed analysis’ as a way of discussing how the writer shapes meaning when considering the keywords of the given view which in this series was team spirit and shared values. Clear focus on the given view allows students to structure a reading that doesn’t just ‘go through’ the extract with paraphrase and list-like analysis of prose methods. Full engagement with the given view encourages a more selective, thorough approach that allows the student to draw together literary analysis and contextual knowledge in a cohesive way. Successful students clearly benefit from exam practice that builds effective time management through focused reading and planning. Careful reading of the question and the preamble is crucial. Reading the preamble helps the student consider the context of the time of setting and publication. Examiners noted that many students grasped the significance of a writer born in 1916 growing up in the inter-war years and who had adult experience of the second World War. Students alert to the 1961 publication date were able to consider the literary context and the revisionary approach to a war that allowed for the massive casualties experienced during the Battle of the Somme. Careful reading of the preamble also allowed students to consider the men who ‘volunteered’ together in pals divisions and the impact of mass casualties on their communities. The best work always considered ‘team spirit’ and ‘shared values’ precisely and did not conflate the two. ‘Team spirit’ was explored through considering rhetorical patterns that stressed the collective nature of the immense preparation for battle through repetition of number and adjectives. Repetition of clauses and listing was seen to reinforce the collective nature of ‘team spirit’. Many confident students considered ‘shared values’ to underpin the military discipline of ‘team spirit’ and discussed the presentation of patriotism and national pride in the extract. The use of the Richard II speech allowed students to consider pastoral, spiritual imagery that they thought was typical of early war sentiments. Some sophisticated responses considered the biblical echoes of the narrator’s sense that they were ‘the chosen people, poised on a lofty height’. The singing of ‘God Save the King’ was carefully considered; many could comment on the significance of collective act of singing, others considered how important the anthem was an act of patriotism and how engrained it was in Edwardian England. Less able students tended to treat the text in isolation and were unable to consider many of the contextual prompts highlighted in the preamble. More assertive responses engaged with the given view through criticising the naïve patriotic attitudes of the author. Some students recognised the 1960s context of publication and felt that the patriotism presented in the extract was atypical of the time. More successful students confidently considered narrative form and recognised the irony and pathos embedded in the presentation of ‘team spirit’ and ‘shared values’ before the historical tragedy of The Battle of the Somme. This work carefully considered the significance of the retrospective first person narrative and explored the imagery with more subtlety. These responses explored how ‘team spirt’ was merely subsumed into a vast mechanised war that was represented through the simile of the ‘iron monster’. Less able students misread the imagery and concluded that this was the force that the soldiers would need to fight against. More assured students recognised that this was ‘The Big Push’ that had been promised as an offensive that would win the war. Confident students explored the true nature of ‘team spirit’ through focusing on specific verb choices; men were mere commodities that would be ‘snatched’ and ‘flung’ into ‘the final holocaust’. Again, the most sophisticated responses explored the religious notion of ‘holocaust’ and sensibly considered the extract in the wider context of the novel’s title, Covenant with Death. More successful extract-based answers • always explored the extract through considering the significance of ‘team spirit and shared values’ • never treated the extract in isolation; had a secure overview of prose structure and perspective as well as using varying contexts to consider the significance of team spirit and shared values’ • did not see prose methods as a simple check list, but through engaging with ‘significance’ purposely considered how the writer shaped meaning. Textual detail was chosen carefully and analysis served to develop an argument rather than as an end in itself • integrated contextual knowledge into the argument rather than using it as an add-on. Always considered the extract and the topic within the shared context of the option • communicated with clarity with an appropriate literary register. Less successful extract-based answers • frequently lost sight of the significance of ‘team spirit and shared values’ and ‘went through’ the extract in a decontextualised way noting prose methods without considering how they shape meaning • either treated the text in isolation, or discussed context in a digressive way which led the student away from the extract • tended to ‘feature spot’ prose methods and sometimes produced over-elaborate readings based on the use of punctuation or misapplied poetic terminology such as ‘volta’ to a prose text • did not read carefully and produced misreadings to support over-assertive ideas • did not communicate clearly and sometimes adopted an over-elaborated style of writing perhaps to create an academic register. Students need to be reminded that the best work communicates complex ideas simply.

Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations

AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression

Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of

erText: In Paper 1, two out of three tasks involve explicit comparison. In Papers 2A and 2B, one out of three tasks is explicitly comparative. The NEA task is also explicitly comparative. In stark contrast, Specification B never asks students to compare one text with another. There are other kinds of comparison involved in Specification A tasks too, of course, such as explicit or implicit comparison within the shared contexts to establish typicality or atypicality. A clear understanding of the task was key to success in this comparative element of section B. Students were asked to compare the significance of team spirit and shared values across two texts from different genres. Well-prepared students clearly familiar with the unchanging format of this task. Successful comparisons explored differences, not just similarities. They considered how the given theme was presented in both texts, focusing on the differing genres and literary methods. Weaker responses relied on content similarities and narrative paraphrasing, ignoring genre differences. Understanding 'significance' is crucial for considering genres, methods, and contexts that create meaning. Successful students used precise literary language appropriate to poetry, drama, and prose. Less successful work often focused on word-level analysis and misapplied poetic terms to drama and prose. Work that was less successful tended to focus more on demonstrating knowledge and understanding of the chosen texts, rather than selecting material relevant to 'team spirit and shared values'. These efforts often involved treating the two texts separately through extensive sections on each individual text, using brief discourse markers such as 'similarly' or 'on the other hand'. In contrast, more thoughtful work seamlessly integrated discussions of both texts and purposefully analysed well-chosen textual details to construct a convincing comparison. To achieve higher marks, students should establish comparative links by thoughtfully and precisely selecting textual details, rather than attempting to demonstrate familiarity with their texts through narrative-driven work that may become digressive. The chosen theme of ‘team spirit and shared values’ was accessible to the majority of students. Importantly, many students produced responses that focused on how ‘team spirit and shared values’ differed and could became a source of conflict. Such work considered conflict within the military hierarchy where ‘team spirit and shared values’ were often very different. The dramatic conflict between Hibbert and Stanhope in Journey’s End was often purposefully considered as Sherriff’s way of presenting the necessity of ‘team spirit’ on the front-line. In The Wipers Times ‘shared values’ was often explored through considering the conflict between Roberts and the military hierarchy represented by Howfield who opposes the newspaper and states that ‘The battlefield is not the place for humour’. Students also compared how presentations of ‘team spirit and shared values’ differ because of time. These responses purposely compared early and later war poetry through a comparison with characters such as Raleigh or Stanhope from Journey’s End, or Burns and Sassoon from Regeneration. Students also successfully compared the differing presentations of home-front and front-line values. Such work considered the ’team spirit’ presented in Jessie Pope’s poetry or the lack of ‘shared values’ that soldiers experience when they are away from the front-line in Regeneration or Birdsong. Successful work shows that understanding different contexts can help explore meaning in a precise and nuanced way. However, many students discuss context in a way that becomes digressive and moves away from close textual analysis. For instance, discussing ‘the shared values’ represented in propaganda and jingoism should be integrated into an analysis of the characterisation of Howfield in The Wipers Times or Hamilton’s poem The Jingo-Woman. Less successful students often focused on individual words rather than considering form and structure. This led to assertive interpretations based on sometimes inaccurate linguistic analysis. In this work there was also a tendency to misapply poetic analysis to other genres. AQA’s Teaching Guide to AO2 offers a better method for understanding how meaning is constructed across genres. https://www.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/as-and-a-level/english-literature-a/teach/teaching-guide-ao2 More successful comparative set text answers: • consider the given view through comparing the two chosen texts • move fluently between texts often exploring difference rather than just similarity • carefully select relevant textual details to support ideas • have a secure understanding of poetic, dramatic and/or prose methods • always link literary analysis to meaning • integrate an understanding of context into literary analysis • can consider how texts may shape meaning in a more tentative fashion when necessary • show awareness of typicality in the literature of WW1 and its aftermath. Less successful comparative set text answers: • lose sight of the given topic and resort to narrative paraphrase • tend to unload ideas often leading to digressive work which can be rushed and incomplete • tend to be assertive and are not supported by well-chosen references • can only ‘feature spot’ sometimes inaccurately and can only link methods to meaning in an assertive unconvincing way • make generalised references to context and typicality that lead to assertive, inaccurate arguments. Secure AO1 is essential when comparing two texts using a central argument. Students who effectively used these AO1 tools often gave more successful responses: • clear introductions and conclusions that focus on the keywords and frame the response • clear paragraphing to build structured comparison • purposeful discourse markers to highlight comparative thinking • clear succinct expression that avoids imprecise, overlong sentences • clear use of topic sentences to guide a purposeful argument. Times is now the only post-2000 drama text. Students are approaching it with greater confidence and understanding of its dramatic methods. Many focused on the ‘team spirit’ between the men, especially the relationship between Roberts and Pearson. Successful responses examined humour thoroughly, seeing it as more than just a coping device. They understood satire as a protest against patriotic home front values and analysed the dramatic presentation of the ironic adverts from the original newspaper. These responses also explored humour and satire in war, comparing the play with satiric poems like Sassoon’s ‘The General’.

Question 01
Feminine Gospels – Carol Ann Duffy
Examine the significance of the collection’s title, Feminine Gospels.
You must write about at least two poems in your answer.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Students might consider:
• the implications of the word ‘feminine’, in terms of the collection’s focus on sharing women’s
stories, possibly as a reaction to women being traditionally side-lined by men’s actions and
decisions throughout history, eg ‘Loud’, ‘Tall’, ‘Beautiful’, ‘Work’ and ‘History’
• the implications of the word ‘gospels’ in terms of its promising a new kind of teaching or revelation,
eg as shown in poems that present a revisionist retelling of the biblical gospels of Matthew, Mark,
Luke and John
• Duffy’s decision to dedicate the collection to her four brothers, as listeners rather than authors of

Read the Insert. Answer both questions in this section.
Read the Insert carefully. It is taken from Restless, a novel by William Boyd, published in 2006. The
extract is set in London during World War II, when German air raids were frequent and devastating.
Eva Delectorskaya, a young Russian-born woman working as a spy for the British, has discovered
that her boss, Romer, is a traitor. Now living in hiding, Eva knows that Romer will kill her to prevent
her revealing his betrayal. The extract begins with Eva planning how to escape from Romer
permanently.
Explore the significance of the struggle for identity in this extract.
Remember to include in your answer relevant detailed analysis of the ways that Boyd
shapes meanings.
[25 marks]
msText:
Question 05
Explore the significance of the struggle for identity in this extract.
Remember to include in your answer relevant detailed analysis of the ways that Boyd shapes
meanings.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Focus might be on:
• the World War II time period – the action taking place on the Home Front in London at the height of
the Blitz, just before the beginning of the Modern Times synchronic time period
• the fact that Eva’s wartime experience fighting for the freedom of others has now become a
desperate personal struggle to assume a new identity
• Eva’s struggle for personal freedom and a new identity as analogous to that of the countries
attempting to achieve autonomy and self-determination on a global scale; possibly the idea that it
is easier to focus on the fate of one individual rather than millions
• issues of gender, power, nationality and class, given Eva’s original Russian birth and background,
and her assumption of the stolen identity of an English girl; the contrasting names ‘Eva
Delectorskaya’ and ‘Sally Fairchild’ may be seen as significant, with Sally’s name perhaps seen as
suggesting a fresh start; reference may be made to the future Cold War, which will further separate
Eva from her country of origin
• the difficult moral choices Eva has to make in order to achieve her personal freedom and a new
identity, eg lying to her landlady Mrs Dangerfield and the police; stealing the identity of a dead girl
tragically killed along with the rest of her family; apparently planning to pick up a man in a club who
may be able to protect her
• how Boyd uses Eva’s theft of Sally’s identity to suggest how unstable and at risk individual freedom
can be within society as a whole; the fact that Eva willingly inflicts a minor injury on herself in order
to pass as having survived the air raid that in fact killed Sally Fairchild and her entire family; the
idea that freedom for some may be based upon disaster for others
• etc.
AO4 Explore connections across literary texts
Focus might be on:
• ideas about representations of the struggle for identity as seen in modern literature
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• ideas about how representations of the struggle for identity may be seen to have an impact upon
the ways in which issues key to the context of Modern Times such as class, gender, race, culture
and national identity are received and understood
• etc.
AO2 Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in literary texts
Focus might be on:
• Boyd’s decision to focalise the events through Eva’s point of view while retaining a third-person
stance
• elements typical of the genre of the spy thriller or escape/adventure story
• the cool factual tone used to describe horrific and tragic events; the listing of the five dead
Fairchilds
• use of verisimilitude to add a sense of authenticity; use of specific numbers of the dead and
missing; use of specific locations eg Deptford, Battersea, Rotherhithe, Victoria Station, Whitehall,
the Chelsea Arts Club etc
• aspects of Boyd’s structure, eg Eva’s various journeys to establish her new identity
• the garish description of the bombed-out ruins of Carlisle House; the ‘fuming moonscape’, ‘hills’
and ‘teetering cliffs’ of dereliction
• the symbolism of Eva burning her passport in order to assume a new identity; the symbolic
difference between her old and assumed names
• The persistent threat of Romer and the hints of their former close relationship; his ‘perverse
pleasure in her skills at evasion’
• the way in which Eva behaves in stereotypically ‘feminine’ ways such as weeping and feigning
concussion in order to elicit sympathy; her cleverness in fooling the authorities – the police, the
Home Office etc
• how Boyd’s word choices and syntax within the narrative description suggests the 1940s wartime
context and setting – eg the ‘eligible’ young men she hunts down at various night clubs
• etc.
AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression

• organisation of ideas
• use of appropriate concepts and terminology
• technical accuracy.

authorial methods.
erText: The unseen prose extract has been chosen with a clear beginning and end to enable more thorough analysis. The key words of the given view are intended as a lens through which to view to the extract. Therefore, there is every reason to spend a substantial amount of time analysing the extract given in the light of the stated theme: in this series the struggle for identity. As the extract is always from a novel published after 1945, it is particularly important to write about prose narrative. Precise relevant references to aspects of narrative methods are encouraged. Essential to success in this question is for students to have undertaken sufficient practice in unseen critical analysis, and to avoid irrelevant references to other texts when instructed to write about the significance of the given theme of loneliness and social isolation ‘in this extract’. Whereas less effective responses to William Boyd’s Restless (2006) tended to paraphrase the extract via a ‘narrative-with-text’ approach plus attendant feature-spotting, better responses engaged enthusiastically and skilfully with this text and found plenty of illuminating things to say about her narrative methods. Some writing of exceptionally high quality was seen here, especially when students correctly identified the genre of the text as a historical spy thriller. Better answers, while acknowledging that the extract is only a tiny part of a much longer text, wrote well about its internal structure and cohesion, eg the beginning, development and denouement of the scene. Weaker answers made assertions that showed a basic misunderstanding of the nature of the task, such as claiming that Boyd began writing ‘in media res’ when actually AQA had selected the extract, or stating that his purpose was, for example, ‘to explore male mental health’ through his writing. Clearly the theme of the struggle for identity was selected by AQA for the purposes of this examination and not by Boyd himself nearly twenty years ago. The best answers commented effectively on Boyd’s use of a third-person narrative point of view often focalised through his central protagonist, Eva Delectorskaya. Students who were unable to recognise Boyd’s viewpoint were disadvantaged from the outset, since correctly ascertaining this opened up the overall tone of the extract. It was always a problem to get back on track when this core aspect of the text was misunderstood. Too many students asserted that Boyd’s third-person narrative stance necessarily ‘distanced’ both the reader and (oddly) himself from Eva – a simplistic cliché that showed a lack of close reading. Eva’s thoughts, ideas and actions are tracked throughout the extract; the reader follows her every step of the way from the bombed-out ruins of the East End to the posh cafés of the West End. Readers are capable of empathising with and understanding the motivations and actions of fictional protagonists without the first-person narrative voice being employed. One wonders why any writer would use the third-person stance if it was as useless and retrograde as some students claimed. Less able students with an insecure grasp of context and typicality tended to assert that when Boyd wrote the novel in 2006, he must have been thinking about the aftermath of 9/11, or indeed any major world event or conflict situation they could think of that took place after or around 2000. This type of comment shows a very limited grasp of the contexts of production and reception. Urging protagonist Eva to get a job and become a feminist, or to stop drinking alcohol and trying to find a man, suggested that Boyd’s character was being seen as a real person rather than as a fictional construct; while wondering if Boyd the writer ‘could not identify with Eva because he is a man’ was equally irrelevant and limited. Students who put context before text placed themselves at a disadvantage by making speculative claims that Boyd predicted the 2017 #MeToo movement or the arrival of immigrants from Eastern Europe in the 2000s. Asserting that Boyd was ‘really’ writing about issues from his own day was digressive and impossible to substantiate in their responses. Had they analysed the extract as part of a historical novel set during World War II, their answers would have been far more pertinent, relevant and insightful. More successful extract-based answers: ● look at the whole extract in detail with relevant reference to the presentation of the set topic and its significance – and understand that in this specification, ‘significance’ does not mean ‘relative importance’, but is an invitation to create a sharply focused argument about the possible meanings encoded in the set topic (see also below for more about this key term) ● sustain focus on the extract and the writer’s narrative methods ● make considered and accurate use of contextual factors arising out of the text ● show awareness and understanding of the typicality of the set topic within this shared context. Less successful extract-based answers: ● make sparse use of the extract, or neglect parts of it, or impose one narrow view upon it and attempt to prove its ‘correctness’ ● do not pay attention to the writer’s narrative methods ● write about the characters as though they are real people ● describe or paraphrase the extract ● make inaccurate, unsubstantiated, irrelevant and/or sweeping assertions about context.

erText: In Paper 1, two out of three tasks involve explicit comparison. In Papers 2A and 2B, one out of three tasks is explicitly comparative. The NEA task is also explicitly comparative. In stark contrast, Specification B never asks students to compare one text with another. There are other kinds of comparison involved in Specification A tasks too, of course, such as explicit or implicit comparison within the shared contexts to establish typicality or atypicality. To connect texts successfully within the framework of this question, students must remember that they have been instructed to compare the presentation of the given theme – the struggle for identity - across two texts from different genres. Sometimes even relatively strong candidates did not take full advantage of exploring these differences, and the weakest responses almost always insisted, often very unconvincingly, that their comparative set texts dealt with the given theme in ‘very similar’ ways. Many students defaulted to using the connective ‘similarly’ before going on to make a point that actually pointed to a major difference between the texts. When comparing any two of the three genres of poetry, prose and drama, it is crucial to analyse how they differ. There is no point in asserting that two texts are similar simply because they both deal with the same given theme – all the comparative set texts must do so, or the question could not have been set. The focus of the response must be on presentation, not merely content; the how as much as the what. Previous reports have stressed the importance of being able to explore specific poetic, dramatic and prose methods so that an understanding of how writers operate can be established by the student. Successful responses tend to be marked by an awareness and understanding of the genre under discussion, and that poets, dramatists and novelists have different ways of working. Examiners understand that like is not being compared with like here, so a novelist’s or dramatist’s methods may need more exposition and reference than those of a poet. The challenge for students is to demonstrate that different terminology and different metrics will be needed to measure the effects of different genre methods. Many students connected texts by putting texts side by side and going from one to the other in a linear fashion. However, the best responses were fully comparative where detailed similarities and differences were closely explored. The latter is a higher order skill that opens up the higher reaches of the mark scheme. Better students worked through thoughtfully developed links between their texts that focused on how the writers’ poetic, narrative or dramatic methods worked to illuminate the theme of the struggle for identity. Crucially, they also clearly identified the nature of this topic as shown within their texts, eg in relation to the role of women, sexuality, class, race. Less able students tended to off-load preconceived ideas about context and typicality without successfully relating them to the given theme – and/or their responses failed to clarify exactly how and where the struggle for identity was to be seen within their chosen texts. At times, a bolted-on contextual overlay swamped the chosen texts, with some students losing focus that this examination is in English Literature (not history, politics, psychology or sociology). Potted histories of various waves of feminism or the struggle for civil rights, for example, are not asked for or required. When exploring their comparative set texts in an Open Book examination, accurate textual detail is crucial; well-chosen aspects of authorial method must form the bedrock of any successful comparison. Students who adopt a lexical approach to AO2 often self-penalise. Writing two or three paragraphs about, for example, the impact on the audience of Tennessee Williams’s use of alliteration in a single stage direction from A Streetcar Named Desire is not a productive mode of literary analysis. Moreover, it is remarkable how many of the students who choose this unhelpful ‘dissection’ approach inevitably do not succeed in getting the basics right; there were numerous over-confident identifications of a specific part of speech in which ‘the adjective’ was in fact a noun, pronoun or adverb. The resultant display is not of knowledge and understanding but the exact opposite. AQA’s Teaching Guide to AO2 offers a clear way into thinking about the different ways in which meaning is shaped across the three different genres. https://www.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/as-and-a-level/english-literature-a/teach/teaching- guide-ao2 More successful comparative set text answers: ● look at both texts with the question focus of the struggle for identity in mind ● sustain a comparative approach ● support relevant readings with specific textual details ● analyse poetic, dramatic and/or prose methods by linking them to meaning, in a tentative fashion where necessary ● apply context in a considered way, again being suitably tentative rather than assertively definitive ● show awareness of typicality in the literature of modern times. Less successful comparative set text answers: ● work through the texts a narrative/descriptive manner, often losing sight of the specific task focus of the struggle for identity ● leave ideas undeveloped and unsupported ● assert over-confident, generalised and speculative interpretations ● describe poetic, dramatic and/or prose methods in isolation, with no reference to meaning, or simply assert an unconvincing link to an alleged meaning ● label methods and word classes inaccurately ● make sweeping, simplistic or inaccurate statements about context and/or typicality in the literature of modern times. Some students used an ornate style of writing which was presumably felt to be ‘academic’, but which, in its convoluted syntax and elaborate (and often inaccurate) word choices, actually impeded the clear communication of meaning. With two texts to consider and an argument to build, comparisons are best constructed with the tools of clear AO1 in a way that signals the argument to the reader and guides them accordingly: ● introductions and conclusions ● clean sentences ● clear paragraphs ● paragraphs that begin with topic sentences that relate back to the central theme ● discourse markers to signal similarity and difference. On the whole, however, many excellent comparative essays were seen that analysed how each text represented the theme of changing social attitudes in terms of attitudes, beliefs, values, norms and ethics. Truly original and fascinating connections were traced across the chosen texts in relation to a wide variety of possible issues and areas that might give rise to changing social attitudes, including gender, class, race, sexuality, religion and mental health. Some students compared how specific characters within their texts respond to the struggle for identity in various ways, and acknowledged how these may be viewed very differently over time. As with this type of very open question in previous examination series, the best answers here were simply outstanding and illuminated the chosen comparative texts in innovative, complex and fascinating ways.

the line is ‘Cemeteries’, which may represent her living death in the asylum

ridden by both Blanche and Stella
• that both Blanche and Stella use the metaphor of the streetcar explicitly when talking to each other
in Scene IV; Stella is glad to ride the ‘streetcar’ of desire with Stanley, but Blanche acknowledges
desire as the source of all her troubles: ‘it brought me here, where I’m not wanted, and where I’m
ashamed to be’
• the way in which the title signals Williams’ presentation of desire as a motivating force among all
three of the major characters in a notably frank and modern way for the late 1940s context of
production
• the tragic genre
• the possible impact of particular production(s) on the interpretation of the question
• etc.

• dramatic representations of aspects of desire, class and culture as seen in modern literature
• etc.

literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:

• the extent to which the title is embedded in the play’s specific contemporary context of production,
and how responses to the text then and now can reflect changing attitudes over time
• etc.

text:
Read the Insert. Answer both questions in this section.
Read the Insert carefully. It is taken from Restless, a novel by William Boyd, published in 2006. The
extract is set in London during World War II, when German air raids were frequent and devastating.
Eva Delectorskaya, a young Russian-born woman working as a spy for the British, has discovered
that her boss, Romer, is a traitor. Now living in hiding, Eva knows that Romer will kill her to prevent
her revealing his betrayal. The extract begins with Eva planning how to escape from Romer
permanently.
Explore the significance of the struggle for identity in this extract.
Remember to include in your answer relevant detailed analysis of the ways that Boyd
shapes meanings.
[25 marks]
msText:
Question 11
Explore the significance of the struggle for identity in this extract.
Remember to include in your answer relevant detailed analysis of the ways that Boyd shapes
meanings.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Focus might be on:
• the World War II time period – the action taking place on the Home Front in London at the height of
the Blitz, just before the beginning of the Modern Times synchronic time period
• the fact that Eva’s wartime experience fighting for the freedom of others has now become a
desperate personal struggle to assume a new identity
• Eva’s struggle for personal freedom and a new identity as analogous to that of the countries
attempting to achieve autonomy and self-determination on a global scale; possibly the idea that it
is easier to focus on the fate of one individual rather than millions
• issues of gender, power, nationality and class, given Eva’s original Russian birth and background,
and her assumption of the stolen identity of an English girl; the contrasting names ‘Eva
Delectorskaya’ and ‘Sally Fairchild’ may be seen as significant, with Sally’s name perhaps seen as
suggesting a fresh start; reference may be made to the future Cold War, which will further separate
Eva from her country of origin
• the difficult moral choices Eva has to make in order to achieve her personal freedom and a new
identity, eg lying to her landlady Mrs Dangerfield and the police; stealing the identity of a dead girl
tragically killed along with the rest of her family; apparently planning to pick up a man in a club who
may be able to protect her
• how Boyd uses Eva’s theft of Sally’s identity to suggest how unstable and at risk individual freedom
can be within society as a whole; the fact that Eva willingly inflicts a minor injury on herself in order
to pass as having survived the air raid that in fact killed Sally Fairchild and her entire family; the
idea that freedom for some may be based upon disaster for others
• etc.
AO4 Explore connections across literary texts
Focus might be on:
• ideas about representations of the struggle for identity as seen in modern literature
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• ideas about how representations of the struggle for identity may be seen to have an impact upon
the ways in which issues key to the context of Modern Times such as class, gender, race, culture
and national identity are received and understood
• etc.
AO2 Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in literary texts
Focus might be on:
• Boyd’s decision to focalise the events through Eva’s point of view while retaining a third-person
stance
• elements typical of the genre of the spy thriller or escape/adventure story
• the cool factual tone used to describe horrific and tragic events; the listing of the five dead
Fairchilds
• use of verisimilitude to add a sense of authenticity; use of specific numbers of the dead and
missing; use of specific locations eg Deptford, Battersea, Rotherhithe, Victoria Station, Whitehall,
the Chelsea Arts Club etc
• aspects of Boyd’s structure, eg Eva’s various journeys to establish her new identity
• the garish description of the bombed-out ruins of Carlisle House; the ‘fuming moonscape’, ‘hills’
and ‘teetering cliffs’ of dereliction
• the symbolism of Eva burning her passport in order to assume a new identity; the symbolic
difference between her old and assumed names
• The persistent threat of Romer and the hints of their former close relationship; his ‘perverse
pleasure in her skills at evasion’
• the way in which Eva behaves in stereotypically ‘feminine’ ways such as weeping and feigning
concussion in order to elicit sympathy; her cleverness in fooling the authorities – the police, the
Home Office etc
• how Boyd’s word choices and syntax within the narrative description suggests the 1940s wartime
context and setting – eg the ‘eligible’ young men she hunts down at various night clubs
• etc.
AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression
• quality of argument
• organisation of ideas
• use of appropriate concepts and terminology
• technical accuracy.
Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of
authorial methods.
erText: The unseen prose extract has been chosen with a clear beginning and end to enable more thorough analysis. The key words of the given view are intended as a lens through which to view to the extract. Therefore, there is every reason to spend a substantial amount of time analysing the extract given in the light of the stated theme: in this series the struggle for identity. As the extract is always from a novel published after 1945, it is particularly important to write about prose narrative. Precise relevant references to aspects of narrative methods are encouraged. Essential to success in this question is for students to have undertaken sufficient practice in unseen critical analysis, and to avoid irrelevant references to other texts when instructed to write about the significance of the given theme of loneliness and social isolation ‘in this extract’. Whereas less effective responses to William Boyd’s Restless (2006) tended to paraphrase the extract via a ‘narrative-with-text’ approach plus attendant feature-spotting, better responses engaged enthusiastically and skilfully with this text and found plenty of illuminating things to say about her narrative methods. Some writing of exceptionally high quality was seen here, especially when students correctly identified the genre of the text as a historical spy thriller. Better answers, while acknowledging that the extract is only a tiny part of a much longer text, wrote well about its internal structure and cohesion, eg the beginning, development and denouement of the scene. Weaker answers made assertions that showed a basic misunderstanding of the nature of the task, such as claiming that Boyd began writing ‘in media res’ when actually AQA had selected the extract, or stating that his purpose was, for example, ‘to explore male mental health’ through his writing. Clearly the theme of the struggle for identity was selected by AQA for the purposes of this examination and not by Boyd himself nearly twenty years ago. The best answers commented effectively on Boyd’s use of a third-person narrative point of view often focalised through his central protagonist, Eva Delectorskaya. Students who were unable to recognise Boyd’s viewpoint were disadvantaged from the outset, since correctly ascertaining this opened up the overall tone of the extract. It was always a problem to get back on track when this core aspect of the text was misunderstood. Too many students asserted that Boyd’s third-person narrative stance necessarily ‘distanced’ both the reader and (oddly) himself from Eva – a simplistic cliché that showed a lack of close reading. Eva’s thoughts, ideas and actions are tracked throughout the extract; the reader follows her every step of the way from the bombed-out ruins of the East End to the posh cafés of the West End. Readers are capable of empathising with and understanding the motivations and actions of fictional protagonists without the first-person narrative voice being employed. One wonders why any writer would use the third-person stance if it was as useless and retrograde as some students claimed. Less able students with an insecure grasp of context and typicality tended to assert that when Boyd wrote the novel in 2006, he must have been thinking about the aftermath of 9/11, or indeed any major world event or conflict situation they could think of that took place after or around 2000. This type of comment shows a very limited grasp of the contexts of production and reception. Urging protagonist Eva to get a job and become a feminist, or to stop drinking alcohol and trying to find a man, suggested that Boyd’s character was being seen as a real person rather than as a fictional construct; while wondering if Boyd the writer ‘could not identify with Eva because he is a man’ was equally irrelevant and limited. Students who put context before text placed themselves at a disadvantage by making speculative claims that Boyd predicted the 2017 #MeToo movement or the arrival of immigrants from Eastern Europe in the 2000s. Asserting that Boyd was ‘really’ writing about issues from his own day was digressive and impossible to substantiate in their responses. Had they analysed the extract as part of a historical novel set during World War II, their answers would have been far more pertinent, relevant and insightful. More successful extract-based answers: ● look at the whole extract in detail with relevant reference to the presentation of the set topic and its significance – and understand that in this specification, ‘significance’ does not mean ‘relative importance’, but is an invitation to create a sharply focused argument about the possible meanings encoded in the set topic (see also below for more about this key term) ● sustain focus on the extract and the writer’s narrative methods ● make considered and accurate use of contextual factors arising out of the text ● show awareness and understanding of the typicality of the set topic within this shared context. Less successful extract-based answers: ● make sparse use of the extract, or neglect parts of it, or impose one narrow view upon it and attempt to prove its ‘correctness’ ● do not pay attention to the writer’s narrative methods ● write about the characters as though they are real people ● describe or paraphrase the extract ● make inaccurate, unsubstantiated, irrelevant and/or sweeping assertions about context.

Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations

methods
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• differing representations of the struggle for identity and its possible effects and impact
• the psychological effects of the struggle for identity
• an analytical comparison of characters who respond to the struggle for identity in various ways
• how the struggle for identity may be viewed differently over time
• how the theme of the struggle for identity contributes to a text or texts as a whole
• etc.
AO2 Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in literary texts
Focus might be on:
• methods of presenting and explaining the reasons for the prevalence and significance of the theme
of the struggle for identity in modern literature
• possible purposes and effects of the presentation of the struggle for identity
• prose methods such as: narrative structure; point of view; chronology; use of dialogue; indirect
speech; development of settings; ways of influencing the readers’ response to character and
incident
• dramatic methods such as: explicit structural devices; dramatic irony; stage directions; indirect
ways of communicating the writers’ messages and ideas; naturalistic, non-naturalistic,
expressionist and other styles of representing character, incident and narrative
• poetic methods such as: types of verse form; explicit and implicit structural features; use of tropes
for rhetorical effect; use of aural devices for rhetorical effect; elliptical use of language
• etc.
AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression
• quality of argument

Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of
authorial methods.
erText: In Paper 1, two out of three tasks involve explicit comparison. In Papers 2A and 2B, one out of three tasks is explicitly comparative. The NEA task is also explicitly comparative. In stark contrast, Specification B never asks students to compare one text with another. There are other kinds of comparison involved in Specification A tasks too, of course, such as explicit or implicit comparison within the shared contexts to establish typicality or atypicality. To connect texts successfully within the framework of this question, students must remember that they have been instructed to compare the presentation of the given theme – the struggle for identity - across two texts from different genres. Sometimes even relatively strong candidates did not take full advantage of exploring these differences, and the weakest responses almost always insisted, often very unconvincingly, that their comparative set texts dealt with the given theme in ‘very similar’ ways. Many students defaulted to using the connective ‘similarly’ before going on to make a point that actually pointed to a major difference between the texts. When comparing any two of the three genres of poetry, prose and drama, it is crucial to analyse how they differ. There is no point in asserting that two texts are similar simply because they both deal with the same given theme – all the comparative set texts must do so, or the question could not have been set. The focus of the response must be on presentation, not merely content; the how as much as the what. Previous reports have stressed the importance of being able to explore specific poetic, dramatic and prose methods so that an understanding of how writers operate can be established by the student. Successful responses tend to be marked by an awareness and understanding of the genre under discussion, and that poets, dramatists and novelists have different ways of working. Examiners understand that like is not being compared with like here, so a novelist’s or dramatist’s methods may need more exposition and reference than those of a poet. The challenge for students is to demonstrate that different terminology and different metrics will be needed to measure the effects of different genre methods. Many students connected texts by putting texts side by side and going from one to the other in a linear fashion. However, the best responses were fully comparative where detailed similarities and differences were closely explored. The latter is a higher order skill that opens up the higher reaches of the mark scheme. Better students worked through thoughtfully developed links between their texts that focused on how the writers’ poetic, narrative or dramatic methods worked to illuminate the theme of the struggle for identity. Crucially, they also clearly identified the nature of this topic as shown within their texts, eg in relation to the role of women, sexuality, class, race. Less able students tended to off-load preconceived ideas about context and typicality without successfully relating them to the given theme – and/or their responses failed to clarify exactly how and where the struggle for identity was to be seen within their chosen texts. At times, a bolted-on contextual overlay swamped the chosen texts, with some students losing focus that this examination is in English Literature (not history, politics, psychology or sociology). Potted histories of various waves of feminism or the struggle for civil rights, for example, are not asked for or required. When exploring their comparative set texts in an Open Book examination, accurate textual detail is crucial; well-chosen aspects of authorial method must form the bedrock of any successful comparison. Students who adopt a lexical approach to AO2 often self-penalise. Writing two or three paragraphs about, for example, the impact on the audience of Tennessee Williams’s use of alliteration in a single stage direction from A Streetcar Named Desire is not a productive mode of literary analysis. Moreover, it is remarkable how many of the students who choose this unhelpful ‘dissection’ approach inevitably do not succeed in getting the basics right; there were numerous over-confident identifications of a specific part of speech in which ‘the adjective’ was in fact a noun, pronoun or adverb. The resultant display is not of knowledge and understanding but the exact opposite. AQA’s Teaching Guide to AO2 offers a clear way into thinking about the different ways in which meaning is shaped across the three different genres. https://www.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/as-and-a-level/english-literature-a/teach/teaching- guide-ao2 More successful comparative set text answers: ● look at both texts with the question focus of the struggle for identity in mind ● sustain a comparative approach ● support relevant readings with specific textual details ● analyse poetic, dramatic and/or prose methods by linking them to meaning, in a tentative fashion where necessary ● apply context in a considered way, again being suitably tentative rather than assertively definitive ● show awareness of typicality in the literature of modern times. Less successful comparative set text answers: ● work through the texts a narrative/descriptive manner, often losing sight of the specific task focus of the struggle for identity ● leave ideas undeveloped and unsupported ● assert over-confident, generalised and speculative interpretations ● describe poetic, dramatic and/or prose methods in isolation, with no reference to meaning, or simply assert an unconvincing link to an alleged meaning ● label methods and word classes inaccurately ● make sweeping, simplistic or inaccurate statements about context and/or typicality in the literature of modern times. Some students used an ornate style of writing which was presumably felt to be ‘academic’, but which, in its convoluted syntax and elaborate (and often inaccurate) word choices, actually impeded the clear communication of meaning. With two texts to consider and an argument to build, comparisons are best constructed with the tools of clear AO1 in a way that signals the argument to the reader and guides them accordingly: ● introductions and conclusions ● clean sentences ● clear paragraphs ● paragraphs that begin with topic sentences that relate back to the central theme ● discourse markers to signal similarity and difference. On the whole, however, many excellent comparative essays were seen that analysed how each text represented the theme of changing social attitudes in terms of attitudes, beliefs, values, norms and ethics. Truly original and fascinating connections were traced across the chosen texts in relation to a wide variety of possible issues and areas that might give rise to changing social attitudes, including gender, class, race, sexuality, religion and mental health. Some students compared how specific characters within their texts respond to the struggle for identity in various ways, and acknowledged how these may be viewed very differently over time. As with this type of very open question in previous examination series, the best answers here were simply outstanding and illuminated the chosen comparative texts in innovative, complex and fascinating ways.

Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Students might consider:
• Swift’s presentation of Tom and Mary Crick as childhood sweethearts in the past, and the centrality

• the sadness of Tom and Mary living with the consequences of their past actions; the significance of
Mary’s infertility being the result of an abortion as a 15-year-old girl

shared past and fall from grace

her to a historical character from the French Revolution in having ‘committed a revolutionary act’
(stealing a baby)
• the irony of Mary turning to religion again as once she tried to escape her strict father’s oppressive

God
• Mary’s return to the religious teaching of her strict father, and her belief that the stolen baby is a gift
from God
• Tom’s ‘betrayal’ of Mary and his subsequent grief over her breakdown and committal to a mental

• that Tom may be seen as having ‘imprisoned’ Mary for her actions, just as her father once did after

Read the Insert. Answer both questions in this section.
Read the Insert carefully. It is taken from Restless, a novel by William Boyd, published in 2006. The
extract is set in London during World War II, when German air raids were frequent and devastating.
Eva Delectorskaya, a young Russian-born woman working as a spy for the British, has discovered
that her boss, Romer, is a traitor. Now living in hiding, Eva knows that Romer will kill her to prevent
her revealing his betrayal. The extract begins with Eva planning how to escape from Romer
permanently.
Explore the significance of the struggle for identity in this extract.
Remember to include in your answer relevant detailed analysis of the ways that Boyd
shapes meanings.
[25 marks]
msText:
Question 17
Explore the significance of the struggle for identity in this extract.
Remember to include in your answer relevant detailed analysis of the ways that Boyd shapes
meanings.
[25 marks]
Possible content:
Please refer to pages 4 to 7.
AO5 Explore literary texts informed by different interpretations
Focus might be on:
• the World War II time period – the action taking place on the Home Front in London at the height of
the Blitz, just before the beginning of the Modern Times synchronic time period
• the fact that Eva’s wartime experience fighting for the freedom of others has now become a
desperate personal struggle to assume a new identity
• Eva’s struggle for personal freedom and a new identity as analogous to that of the countries
attempting to achieve autonomy and self-determination on a global scale; possibly the idea that it
is easier to focus on the fate of one individual rather than millions
• issues of gender, power, nationality and class, given Eva’s original Russian birth and background,
and her assumption of the stolen identity of an English girl; the contrasting names ‘Eva
Delectorskaya’ and ‘Sally Fairchild’ may be seen as significant, with Sally’s name perhaps seen as
suggesting a fresh start; reference may be made to the future Cold War, which will further separate
Eva from her country of origin
• the difficult moral choices Eva has to make in order to achieve her personal freedom and a new
identity, eg lying to her landlady Mrs Dangerfield and the police; stealing the identity of a dead girl
tragically killed along with the rest of her family; apparently planning to pick up a man in a club who
may be able to protect her
• how Boyd uses Eva’s theft of Sally’s identity to suggest how unstable and at risk individual freedom
can be within society as a whole; the fact that Eva willingly inflicts a minor injury on herself in order
to pass as having survived the air raid that in fact killed Sally Fairchild and her entire family; the
idea that freedom for some may be based upon disaster for others
• etc.
AO4 Explore connections across literary texts
Focus might be on:
• ideas about representations of the struggle for identity as seen in modern literature
• etc.
AO3 Demonstrate understanding of the significance and influence of the contexts in which
literary texts are written and received
Focus might be on:
• ideas about how representations of the struggle for identity may be seen to have an impact upon
the ways in which issues key to the context of Modern Times such as class, gender, race, culture
and national identity are received and understood
• etc.
AO2 Analyse ways in which meanings are shaped in literary texts
Focus might be on:
• Boyd’s decision to focalise the events through Eva’s point of view while retaining a third-person
stance
• elements typical of the genre of the spy thriller or escape/adventure story
• the cool factual tone used to describe horrific and tragic events; the listing of the five dead
Fairchilds
• use of verisimilitude to add a sense of authenticity; use of specific numbers of the dead and
missing; use of specific locations eg Deptford, Battersea, Rotherhithe, Victoria Station, Whitehall,
the Chelsea Arts Club etc
• aspects of Boyd’s structure, eg Eva’s various journeys to establish her new identity
• the garish description of the bombed-out ruins of Carlisle House; the ‘fuming moonscape’, ‘hills’
and ‘teetering cliffs’ of dereliction
• the symbolism of Eva burning her passport in order to assume a new identity; the symbolic
difference between her old and assumed names
• The persistent threat of Romer and the hints of their former close relationship; his ‘perverse
pleasure in her skills at evasion’
• the way in which Eva behaves in stereotypically ‘feminine’ ways such as weeping and feigning
concussion in order to elicit sympathy; her cleverness in fooling the authorities – the police, the
Home Office etc
• how Boyd’s word choices and syntax within the narrative description suggests the 1940s wartime
context and setting – eg the ‘eligible’ young men she hunts down at various night clubs
• etc.
AO1 Articulate informed, personal and creative responses to literary texts, using associated
concepts and terminology, and coherent, accurate written expression

• organisation of ideas
• use of appropriate concepts and terminology
• technical accuracy.
Accept any valid interpretations, any valid comments on contexts and any valid discussion of
authorial methods.
erText: The unseen prose extract has been chosen with a clear beginning and end to enable more thorough analysis. The key words of the given view are intended as a lens through which to view to the extract. Therefore, there is every reason to spend a substantial amount of time analysing the extract given in the light of the stated theme: in this series the struggle for identity. As the extract is always from a novel published after 1945, it is particularly important to write about prose narrative. Precise relevant references to aspects of narrative methods are encouraged. Essential to success in this question is for students to have undertaken sufficient practice in unseen critical analysis, and to avoid irrelevant references to other texts when instructed to write about the significance of the given theme of loneliness and social isolation ‘in this extract’. Whereas less effective responses to William Boyd’s Restless (2006) tended to paraphrase the extract via a ‘narrative-with-text’ approach plus attendant feature-spotting, better responses engaged enthusiastically and skilfully with this text and found plenty of illuminating things to say about her narrative methods. Some writing of exceptionally high quality was seen here, especially when students correctly identified the genre of the text as a historical spy thriller. Better answers, while acknowledging that the extract is only a tiny part of a much longer text, wrote well about its internal structure and cohesion, eg the beginning, development and denouement of the scene. Weaker answers made assertions that showed a basic misunderstanding of the nature of the task, such as claiming that Boyd began writing ‘in media res’ when actually AQA had selected the extract, or stating that his purpose was, for example, ‘to explore male mental health’ through his writing. Clearly the theme of the struggle for identity was selected by AQA for the purposes of this examination and not by Boyd himself nearly twenty years ago. The best answers commented effectively on Boyd’s use of a third-person narrative point of view often focalised through his central protagonist, Eva Delectorskaya. Students who were unable to recognise Boyd’s viewpoint were disadvantaged from the outset, since correctly ascertaining this opened up the overall tone of the extract. It was always a problem to get back on track when this core aspect of the text was misunderstood. Too many students asserted that Boyd’s third-person narrative stance necessarily ‘distanced’ both the reader and (oddly) himself from Eva – a simplistic cliché that showed a lack of close reading. Eva’s thoughts, ideas and actions are tracked throughout the extract; the reader follows her every step of the way from the bombed-out ruins of the East End to the posh cafés of the West End. Readers are capable of empathising with and understanding the motivations and actions of fictional protagonists without the first-person narrative voice being employed. One wonders why any writer would use the third-person stance if it was as useless and retrograde as some students claimed. Less able students with an insecure grasp of context and typicality tended to assert that when Boyd wrote the novel in 2006, he must have been thinking about the aftermath of 9/11, or indeed any major world event or conflict situation they could think of that took place after or around 2000. This type of comment shows a very limited grasp of the contexts of production and reception. Urging protagonist Eva to get a job and become a feminist, or to stop drinking alcohol and trying to find a man, suggested that Boyd’s character was being seen as a real person rather than as a fictional construct; while wondering if Boyd the writer ‘could not identify with Eva because he is a man’ was equally irrelevant and limited. Students who put context before text placed themselves at a disadvantage by making speculative claims that Boyd predicted the 2017 #MeToo movement or the arrival of immigrants from Eastern Europe in the 2000s. Asserting that Boyd was ‘really’ writing about issues from his own day was digressive and impossible to substantiate in their responses. Had they analysed the extract as part of a historical novel set during World War II, their answers would have been far more pertinent, relevant and insightful. More successful extract-based answers: ● look at the whole extract in detail with relevant reference to the presentation of the set topic and its significance – and understand that in this specification, ‘significance’ does not mean ‘relative importance’, but is an invitation to create a sharply focused argument about the possible meanings encoded in the set topic (see also below for more about this key term) ● sustain focus on the extract and the writer’s narrative methods ● make considered and accurate use of contextual factors arising out of the text ● show awareness and understanding of the typicality of the set topic within this shared context. Less successful extract-based answers: ● make sparse use of the extract, or neglect parts of it, or impose one narrow view upon it and attempt to prove its ‘correctness’ ● do not pay attention to the writer’s narrative methods ● write about the characters as though they are real people ● describe or paraphrase the extract ● make inaccurate, unsubstantiated, irrelevant and/or sweeping assertions about context.

erText: In Paper 1, two out of three tasks involve explicit comparison. In Papers 2A and 2B, one out of three tasks is explicitly comparative. The NEA task is also explicitly comparative. In stark contrast, Specification B never asks students to compare one text with another. There are other kinds of comparison involved in Specification A tasks too, of course, such as explicit or implicit comparison within the shared contexts to establish typicality or atypicality. To connect texts successfully within the framework of this question, students must remember that they have been instructed to compare the presentation of the given theme – the struggle for identity - across two texts from different genres. Sometimes even relatively strong candidates did not take full advantage of exploring these differences, and the weakest responses almost always insisted, often very unconvincingly, that their comparative set texts dealt with the given theme in ‘very similar’ ways. Many students defaulted to using the connective ‘similarly’ before going on to make a point that actually pointed to a major difference between the texts. When comparing any two of the three genres of poetry, prose and drama, it is crucial to analyse how they differ. There is no point in asserting that two texts are similar simply because they both deal with the same given theme – all the comparative set texts must do so, or the question could not have been set. The focus of the response must be on presentation, not merely content; the how as much as the what. Previous reports have stressed the importance of being able to explore specific poetic, dramatic and prose methods so that an understanding of how writers operate can be established by the student. Successful responses tend to be marked by an awareness and understanding of the genre under discussion, and that poets, dramatists and novelists have different ways of working. Examiners understand that like is not being compared with like here, so a novelist’s or dramatist’s methods may need more exposition and reference than those of a poet. The challenge for students is to demonstrate that different terminology and different metrics will be needed to measure the effects of different genre methods. Many students connected texts by putting texts side by side and going from one to the other in a linear fashion. However, the best responses were fully comparative where detailed similarities and differences were closely explored. The latter is a higher order skill that opens up the higher reaches of the mark scheme. Better students worked through thoughtfully developed links between their texts that focused on how the writers’ poetic, narrative or dramatic methods worked to illuminate the theme of the struggle for identity. Crucially, they also clearly identified the nature of this topic as shown within their texts, eg in relation to the role of women, sexuality, class, race. Less able students tended to off-load preconceived ideas about context and typicality without successfully relating them to the given theme – and/or their responses failed to clarify exactly how and where the struggle for identity was to be seen within their chosen texts. At times, a bolted-on contextual overlay swamped the chosen texts, with some students losing focus that this examination is in English Literature (not history, politics, psychology or sociology). Potted histories of various waves of feminism or the struggle for civil rights, for example, are not asked for or required. When exploring their comparative set texts in an Open Book examination, accurate textual detail is crucial; well-chosen aspects of authorial method must form the bedrock of any successful comparison. Students who adopt a lexical approach to AO2 often self-penalise. Writing two or three paragraphs about, for example, the impact on the audience of Tennessee Williams’s use of alliteration in a single stage direction from A Streetcar Named Desire is not a productive mode of literary analysis. Moreover, it is remarkable how many of the students who choose this unhelpful ‘dissection’ approach inevitably do not succeed in getting the basics right; there were numerous over-confident identifications of a specific part of speech in which ‘the adjective’ was in fact a noun, pronoun or adverb. The resultant display is not of knowledge and understanding but the exact opposite. AQA’s Teaching Guide to AO2 offers a clear way into thinking about the different ways in which meaning is shaped across the three different genres. https://www.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/as-and-a-level/english-literature-a/teach/teaching- guide-ao2 More successful comparative set text answers: ● look at both texts with the question focus of the struggle for identity in mind ● sustain a comparative approach ● support relevant readings with specific textual details ● analyse poetic, dramatic and/or prose methods by linking them to meaning, in a tentative fashion where necessary ● apply context in a considered way, again being suitably tentative rather than assertively definitive ● show awareness of typicality in the literature of modern times. Less successful comparative set text answers: ● work through the texts a narrative/descriptive manner, often losing sight of the specific task focus of the struggle for identity ● leave ideas undeveloped and unsupported ● assert over-confident, generalised and speculative interpretations ● describe poetic, dramatic and/or prose methods in isolation, with no reference to meaning, or simply assert an unconvincing link to an alleged meaning ● label methods and word classes inaccurately ● make sweeping, simplistic or inaccurate statements about context and/or typicality in the literature of modern times. Some students used an ornate style of writing which was presumably felt to be ‘academic’, but which, in its convoluted syntax and elaborate (and often inaccurate) word choices, actually impeded the clear communication of meaning. With two texts to consider and an argument to build, comparisons are best constructed with the tools of clear AO1 in a way that signals the argument to the reader and guides them accordingly: ● introductions and conclusions ● clean sentences ● clear paragraphs ● paragraphs that begin with topic sentences that relate back to the central theme ● discourse markers to signal similarity and difference. On the whole, however, many excellent comparative essays were seen that analysed how each text represented the theme of changing social attitudes in terms of attitudes, beliefs, values, norms and ethics. Truly original and fascinating connections were traced across the chosen texts in relation to a wide variety of possible issues and areas that might give rise to changing social attitudes, including gender, class, race, sexuality, religion and mental health. Some students compared how specific characters within their texts respond to the struggle for identity in various ways, and acknowledged how these may be viewed very differently over time. As with this type of very open question in previous examination series, the best answers here were simply outstanding and illuminated the chosen comparative texts in innovative, complex and fascinating ways.
